subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCREPANCY IN ANSWER GIVEN BY SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Last Thursday, February 27, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) may have- unintentionally, I am sure-left ambiguities on the record with respect to questions asked by me. I wish to bring these briefly to the attention of the House so that the Solicitor General, if he deems it necessary, will have the opportunity to correct Hansard in this respect.
As I see it, the discrepancy is as follows. When asked by me whether other federal agencies besides the RCMP were involved in the investigation into dredging operations, the Solicitor General replied, "there are other federal departments involved". I ask Your Honour to keep in mind that I asked about agencies, and not departments. Then later on, as reported at page 3624 of Hansard, the Solicitor General took the opportunity to answer more fully the question and said:
I was asked whether other agencies were involved in the investigation with respect to the dredging contract in the Quebec City area. I said other agencies were involved.
In point of fact, Mr. Speaker, he did not; he said other federal departments were involved. However, to continue his answer:
Then, the question was: Could you reveal the other agencies? I checked into that, and the answer is that it would interfere with the investigation if we made public the other agencies that we are investigating.
Did he mean that other federal departments are working with the RCMP on their investigation into dredging contracts, or did he mean that federal departments as well as agencies are being investigated by the RCMP in regard to dredging contracts; and is there a difference between "department" and "agency"? That, Mr. Speaker, is my point of order and I hope the Solicitor General can clear it up.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED DISCREPANCY IN ANSWER GIVEN BY SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the same point of order, unfortunately there was a mistake in Hansard on that day. I made every attempt to have it corrected. As a matter of fact, I corrected the blues and Hansard ignored my correction on the blues and put it the way it was originally. I corrected it again. I telephoned Hansard; I had people in my office write them, and so on.
May I clarify the situation. When I said there were other agencies working on this investigation as well, that of course entails other departments because the agencies come under other departments. I was not being explicit. There are agencies of the federal government that come under other federal departments working on this investigation as well. I cannot say any more at this time because it would be contrary to the interests of the investigation. But I stand by the other part of my answer. They are investigating; we are not investigating them. The mistake in Hansard was that it said "we", and it should not.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask leave of the House, seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), to debate a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The matter concerns the tie up of grain shipping on the west coast. subtopic: STUDY OF HEALTH OF MINERS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE-REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STANDARDS FOR AMOUNT OF ASBESTOS FIBRE IN AIR
STUDY OF HEALTH OF MINERS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE-REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STANDARDS FOR AMOUNT OF ASBESTOS FIBRE IN AIR
speechtext:
My question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and arises from answers he gave in the House yesterday to questions concerning the Clinton Creek mine in the Yukon. The minister indicated that the study of that mine showed that there were two to four fibres per millimetre of air and implied that that is a safe level. The report shows that out of 133 fibre counts, 19 were over five fibres per millimetre. Would the minister advise this House if

any studies have been done by his department into the health of the miners in that mine in view of the obvious hazard to those workers in that particular area which this report confirms?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STUDY OF HEALTH OF MINERS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE-REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STANDARDS FOR AMOUNT OF ASBESTOS FIBRE IN AIR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, contrary to what the hon. member said, I did not infer any conclusion from the facts I mentioned in the House yesterday. I just gave him the facts that were available to me and based on the preliminary studies conducted by officials in my department and that of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I am told the studies will be completed in a fortnight or so and my department will then submit them to the Indian Affairs and Northern Development Department for consideration and action.

subtopic: STUDY OF HEALTH OF MINERS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE-REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STANDARDS FOR AMOUNT OF ASBESTOS FIBRE IN AIR
speechtext: I understand that that particular report to which the minister is referring has been in the hands either of his department or of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development since June of last year, and as far as I know there have not been objective studies done up to this point into the health of those miners. In view of the fact that there is nothing that I know of to prevent the minister from bringing in national enforceable standards in terms of asbestos risk, would the minister now advise whether he has any immediate plans to bring forward national enforceable standards, as Britain has had for so many years, for the protection of those persons working in and around asbestos from cancer?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STUDY OF HEALTH OF MINERS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE-REQUEST FOR NATIONAL STANDARDS FOR AMOUNT OF ASBESTOS FIBRE IN AIR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the first place, if the hon. member has a study dating from June last, I would like very much to obtain a copy. speechtext:

A story, published the day before yesterday in the paper Montreal-Matin, has stunned me. It said that the rich pay less income tax. The House resumed, from Wednesday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Whelan that Bill C-50, to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I had before six o'clock last evening I was discussing the amendments proposed, and I ended by saying that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should be ashamed to bring in an amendment to the old stabilization act, presenting it to the farmers as the stabilization plan he has been telling them he is going to bring forth to stabilize agriculture. These amendments are not very great at all, and you could do almost anything under the old act that you can with the amended act. One thing which the minister said in his speech-and I thought at the time I heard him correctly-I would like to read now:
There is also a provision in the bill which some of my colleagues in cabinet suggest gives the Minister of Agriculture a blank cheque to support the food producers of the nation.
That is all he said. He did not go On to say what the provision of this bill was; he left that to the imagination. If he is saying that the bill will now be so written that he can do more than it says, I would respectfully submit that he could have done the same thing under the old stabilization act and really did not need to bring in amendments to do exactly what he is trying to do with these amendments. The minister attended a meeting of the Horticultural Council on Monday morning and told them, among other things:
Nearly 40 per cent of the food we eat, by weight, is fruits and vegetables, or their products. I hope you realize how much impact on the food system your decisions can have.
He went on to explain that the percentage of fruits and vegetables eaten in Canada has gone down in comparison to the amount produced. In other words, the producers are not producing as much today in the way of fruits and vegetables as they used to. He also said that the percentage of fruit canned in Canada is less than it used to be. After giving them these figures, he said:
What do these figures mean? How much of this slide away from self-sufficiency is because Canadians now have more money and are buying a wider variety of tropical and offshore fruits and vegetables? How much of this stems from the fact that our best fruit lands and vegetable soils are being bulldozed for highways and built up into towns? How much of it is due to the limitations of our climate? Are our marketing systems or our production skills lagging behind other parts of the world? Think about this.
Over the years I have thought a lot about what the minister was asking there and I think it is very significant that he left out the question,-"How much of it is due to government policies or lack of government policies in agriculture in Canada, especially in the fruit and vegetable fields?" The next night the Minister of Agriculture went to one of the areas in southern Ontario and made a
Agricultural Stabilization Act
speech to another group, telling them that farmers do not have as much tariff protection as industry; they have only 8 per cent tariff protection while industry, on the average, has 16 per cent. Well do I know this, and we have been concerned in the farm community in Canada because this government over the last few years has been giving concessions in the tariff field for agriculture and we have been losing ground.
I think it is well known, and can be well documented, that this is what has happened. The one thing that comes to my mind is the agreement that was made during the Kennedy round on tariffs, in that over a five-year period the tariff would be taken off apples. Before one year was out, what did the minister of finance of the day do? Mr. Edgar Benson removed the Canadian tariff on apples. He then came to us and said the United States would do the same thing. The United States did nothing of the kind; they did not remove their tariff but, instead, said there was an agreement and they were going to abide by it. That is what they did. As a result of this agreement, we had duty-free apples coming into Canada but had to pay duty on apples going into the United States. This is the kind of thing the government has been doing. There has been a lack of any comprehensive agricultural policy, with no stability in agriculture.
The farmer's favourite expression over the last few years has been, "It will be better next year". As a result of these policies during this time, what did the federal government do? It created a vacuum where there was little or no stability in agriculture in Canada because it had no over-all, comprehensive agricultural policy.
What is happening now? The provinces are moving into this vacuum. Already we find that in British Columbia there is an income insurance scheme. The reason is that the vacuum was there and the province is moving in to do something to help the farmers in British Columbia. The Minister of Agriculture-I notice he is not here-when being interviewed on television a while ago in my province said that the province of British Columbia could not come up with a scheme without him and, that they needed him. He said they were just politicking. But the province has a scheme; it is there and it is working. It covers milk, fruit, hogs and field tomatoes. Negotiations are being carried on in respect of vegetables, table eggs, hatching eggs, sheep and blueberries.
The fact that the beef growers are looking very hard and very long at the British Columbia insurance scheme shows the state of affairs the beef industry is in in British Columbia. These ranchers, these beef producers, over the years have wanted very little government interference. What has happened to them in the past year has caused them to take a look at schemes such as this because they are in dire circumstances. They have borrowed from the banks to the allowable limit. Many of them are almost on the verge of bankruptcy.
What did this government do? It interfered with the beef industry in quite a few ways during the last year, none of which interference was of any use to the ranchers in British Columbia. The minister told me that only 50 per cent of the beef produced would come under his so-called

March 6, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
stabilization scheme last year. I would submit that there was less than 50 per cent in British Columbia. This scheme did not do anything for the producer in British Columbia. Now I say to the Minister of Agriculture-and I see he has returned-that he should take a really good look at the British Columbia income insurance scheme.
Yesterday in his speech the minister said that the provinces were all coming to him, asking when he intended to bring in something in respect of stabilization. I wonder what they will think when they see what he has brought before this House. As I said before, the minister said on television in Kelowna that the British Columbia government could not do anything, so far as an income scheme was concerned, without him or the federal government. He said they were just politicking. That scheme is working.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture last week spent a long time discussing the income insurance scheme. We see now that the Ontario Federation of Agriculture has made a representation to the provincial government in respect of an income scheme. The UPA in Quebec is pressing the Quebec government for an income scheme. The British Columbia insurance scheme is based on the cost of production. This is a real cost of production; it is not similar to the cost of production written into Bill C-41 in respect of stabilization, where the wage to producers is not taken into account, where the interest on investment is not taken into account, and where depreciation and other things are not taken into account. In the British Columbia provincial scheme everything is accounted for, even a living wage for the producer.
Certainly in respect of any scheme such as this, after having the farm credit bill and raising the rate of farm credit to $150,000, a large amount of interest will have to be paid on that $150,000. How can you have any type of scheme without having the interest on the investment included? In the British Columbia scheme the producers can opt in or opt out only once. The scheme continues for five years.
I say that the federal government must become involved in what the provinces are doing. The farmers will not be satisfied with anything less. They are not farming any longer as a way of life. When young people enter farming, they want what everyone else has. They want the type of life everyone else has. They want to be able to live like other working people in Canada. I do not believe they are willing to put in the long hours that were formerly put in by people who were dedicated to farming as a way of life. This bill does not come close to resembling the British Columbia scheme. It is just disaster insurance, especially if it is interpreted as it has been in the past.
It was not necessary to amend this act in order to accomplish a lot more than has been accomplished. Much more could have been accomplished, but it would have had to be done by the cabinet. One must go to the cabinet with hat in hand and obtain its approval. Also, there is a lot of lobbying and politicking. This went on in an effort to get an increase. There was no increase. I know this because I was involved in an effort to get the use of the legislation broadened in the way in which it had been said it could be broadened.
Now we find that even with the minister's blank cheque he still must go to the cabinet in order to have it broad-

ened. I do not think he has a blank cheque at all. He has to do exactly what has been done in respect of the old act. This will mean it will be a cabinet decision. Let us stop for a moment and think about the provinces in Canada having their own schemes. There is one in British Columbia, Ontario is looking very hard at one and Quebec is looking very hard at one. Will these be the same plans? What will the ramifications be when each province is in the income insurance plan field in a way which gives the farmers the stability they want without the federal government being involved?
If these three large producing provinces decide to have stabilization programs of their own, programs that they can afford, what about the provinces that cannot afford to have one? Once again I say that the federal government will have to take a harder look at what is going on in Canada. It will have to listen more closely to what the farmers are saying if it does not want chaos to ensue.
Bill C-50 leaves much to be desired. All other products but those that are designated in the bill are left to the whim of the cabinet. Whether or not they are brought under the act is left to the cabinet to decide. With regard to such products as fruit and vegetables, the minister told the Horticultural Council that they constitute nearly 40 per cent of the foodstuffs consumed by Canadians. Much time will be spent in negotiation and lobbying with regard to these products. Another reason the production of fruit and vegetables has decreased in Canada today is that there is lack of stability in the production and marketing of these products. By the time these products are brought under the protection of the act, a farmer may be out of business or so disillusioned with farming that he considers selling his farm and moving to an urban area.
If 90 per cent support is all a farmer can get or else he has to go hat in hand to the cabinet, then the situation is bad. With regard to regionalism, it is thought that special deals can be made with the provinces provided the provinces and the producers make up the extra amount of money. One wonders what the minister was thinking when he drafted the bill. Perhaps he thought that we should add a provision so that the provincial income insurance programs could be included. This whole issue will become very political. If there is to be any kind of federal plan and if there is to be a different plan in each province, then a formula must be devised so that quick action can be taken, and the long intervals during which a provincial plan is negotiated would thus be avoided.
This government should catch up with the times and implement a federal stabilization plan which will be of benefit to the farmers. It is certain that farmers are the greatest people in Canada. They produce more per person than any industry. However, they are concerned about the present situation because they have a hard time making a living. They do not want to be second-class citizens. They are knowledgeable and hard working people, with production know-how. They want to work the same hours as everyone else, and that means that more people will have to be employed in farming.
Farmers want some stability in the cost of their products, and they are certainly entitled to it. However, this
March 6, 1975

bill does not provide that stability unless a disaster occurs. As I said before, this bill does not even come close to providing the stability which the minister has been saying he will give to farmers. The result of this lack of stability in the price of agricultural products will be that more food shortages will take place in the future.
The other day the minister said in a speech in southern Ontario-the reason I know what he said is that he has been sending all his speeches to my office and I have been reading them just in case I pick up a gem and find he said something different-that we exported $4 billion worth of farm products. However, he neglected to say that the bulk of those exports was made up of prairie wheat, and that if it were not for the export of wheat we would be a net importer of all the other agricultural products, which we almost are at present.
The reason for these food shortages is lack of stability in farming in Canada. We know that there are food shortages in the world. The farmers know that, and they want to produce more food. But they do not want to overproduce and listen to the same lecture that the potato growers in New Brunswick are getting today. Farmers want stability in agriculture. If they do not get it, they will stop producing; they will become less dedicated and work shorter hours. They will produce only what they can use themselves. The other possibility is that in this situation large corporate farms will come into being. They will look after production according to their own production formulas and, as is happening in industry when companies get into trouble, cut down on production. This is exactly what will happen in farming.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part today in this debate on Bill C-50, to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act, first of all I would like to pay what I consider a well deserved tribute to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), even though he is criticized from time to time by Opposition members-after all, that is what they are here for, we cannot blame them- ;since he was appointed, he has done a tremendous job in defending the cause of Canadian farmers in general. I would like to thank him on behalf of young farmers whom he tends to be more particularly willing to help. Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay him tribute because it had been several years since we have had a Minister of Agriculture so thoroughly dedicated to helping farmers. He has travelled throughout Canada from Halifax to Vancouver, accepted almost every invitation to meet farmers, to have talks with them, discuss their problems and above all devise with them solutions to the problems which agriculture is now faced with.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, fits into a global effort by the government, and the Minister of Agriculture especially, to implement a system of supply and reasonable prices for food products which Canadian people need. Since the beginning of the present session, 9 bills dealing with agriculture have been introduced in this House; 2 of them went through third reading and have become part of our Statutes, one is at the report stage one was referred to the Standing Committee of Agriculture. Five other bills,
Agricultural Stabilization Act
among which the one we are now dealing with, are still under study by the House.
Bill C-50 aims at providing producers with better protection. How is that to be achieved? Mr. Speaker, there are three main amendments in that bill which aim at improving the current situation. First of all, the minister wants to reduce from ten to five the number of years on which to establish the average yield of a given commodity.
Second, the minister wants to take 90 per cent of this average income instead of 80 per cent as it is done now. Third, and I think this is the most important proposal now before us, the minister wants to include a rather complex formula, a pegging formula which will take into account the increase in production costs during the last five years and adding this figure to 90 per cent of the average in the last five years.
Obviously, it is a step in the right direction, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I fully support this bill and I urge my colleagues to do the same even if they want to criticize it a little. As such, this bill tends to establish a floor price for farm products. It is not perfect.
Mr. Speaker, I do not like the word stabilization. In my opinion, the word stabilization is not very accurate. I would rather have the bill deal with a guaranteed minimum price and I think that the amendments to the legislation today are precisely meant to set a guaranteed minimum price for farm products, a price which will take in consideration the production costs, the minimum cost of production for a certain commodity evidently including a return on investments as well as a fair salary for the producer.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is also innovating since the minister stated that from now on the support price will be set in advance, that is at the beginning of a year the producers will know for some commodities mentioned in the bill what will eventually be the support price. They will know at the beginning of a year in the case of pork, for example, based on the five previous years and the 90 per cent formula as well as cost index formula, what will be the nimimum price set throughout the year.
It is certainly a big improvement because right now only milk producers are almost assured to know at the beginning of any given year what their revenue will be. Of course, production costs are still unpredictable but among farmers, milk producers are the only ones who know in advance what they will receive for their production of the year. It is the same for virtually no other agricultural producers. The stabilization bill and the proposed amendment are aimed at establishing what I should call a guaranteed minimum price.
Mr. Speaker, that guaranteed minimum price could be obtained by establishing and recognizing a series of standard farms that could be selected throughout the country. We could have capable operators with fairly recent but not necessarily the most modern facilities. Lastly, we could establish our real costs on the basis of those of efficient operators. I do not think it is enough to have economists sitting somewhere in an ivory tower and, when I mention economists, I know that our minister is listening because he does not necessarily trust them all the time. It is not enough then to have economists sitting in ivory towers

Agricultural Stabilization Act
and studying statistics to establish what should be the minimum price of a product.
We absolutely must have units for a given product, in the field, in the provinces, as well in Halifax as in the province of Quebec, in the Prairies as in British Columbia, which units can serve as a reliable proof of the real production costs of certain farm products. From their data we could set support prices which are important since the bill is intended to apply them on a regional basis. Indeed, a minimum price, Mr. Speaker, adopted for a given product, in a given area, could be clearly advantageous for one area but disadvantageous for another.
Here is an example. If the minimum price for producing, let us say, a pig were based on the minimum production cost in a Saskatchewan unit, where farmers can find surplus grains to feed their pigs, and applied to Canada as a whole, it would probably be unfair to the producers of Newfoundland, New Brunswick and British Columbia. That would be unfair for those who have to pay much higher production costs being located farther from the supply sources, and because, owing to the economic context those production units are in, the production costs are much higher, due to the cost of land, services and other costs.
That is why it is necessary to have standard farms established in every province which could be used as sound standards for production costs on which our economists could then calculate the so-called indexation formula on a regional basis. That formula would really reflect the costs on regional basis, so that the producers will not be disadvantaged in some instances, or too advantaged in some others, since that could happen too. If that happened, production would inevitably shift, which might result in overproduction and a subsequent drop in prices.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with a specific area of the dairy industry, because even though the bill does not refer directly to that industry, it does indirectly because it does refer to industrial milk products.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) made one of his typical attacks against the Minister and the Department yesterday. He described in particular the dairy industry's position, saying that our policy had been a disaster, that the Canadian Dairy Commission was in fact a disaster, if I refer to what he said.
Mr. Speaker, I totally object that attitude by the hon. member for Crowfoot, because his statement definitely does not reflect the situation, or at least his words went beyond his thoughts.
I can say that the dairy industry is doing well, although it is facing problems. I also recognize milk producers are facing difficulties. They had the recent hardship of a marked increase in input costs. Fortunately it seems that for a few weeks at least, input costs have been declining, which is very important as far as milk producers are concerned, since they have fixed revenues and they will not go down. Therefore, a decline in input costs will obviously mean better net income for milk producers. I very sincerely hope this will happen, because it will be needed if they are going to stay in production and bring about a recovery in that industry.

It has been said by our friend the hon. member for Crowfoot that the industry was going down the drain. Such is not the case. Some producers quit farming in 1974, which is normal. Some will always quit, but fortunately others will come in, and things look good enough. It could even be said the dairy herd has probably reached a bottom point. Statistics published at the Conference on farming outlooks show that even if there was a slight 3 percent decrease in the dairy herd, there is also a marked increase in the number of replacement heifers.
Since the figures are taken as of June 1 each year, it suggests that on June 1, 1975, we shall have practically the same dairy stock as the one we had in 1973 and I think that the total production figure of 16.8 billion pounds of milk for 1974 is probably a floor production and that in 1975 it will reach 17 billion pounds. There will be such an increase because the quality of the stock is improving. Not only the size of the stock will increase but, as the trend of the last years indicates, the production per cow will improve, resulting in a generally higher milk production for Canada as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, I shall now consider the price to the milk producer. In March 1974, that price was $7.17 a hundred weight pounds of industrial milk. In March 1975, one year later, it is $10.02, following three adjustments made in 1974 and the recent increase announced in February.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, the price of industrial milk increased by 40 per cent. I note, and I am sure that my colleagues will do the same, that such an increase is good, and that even if it did not solve all the problems of the dairy industry, I think we can be proud of the efforts made by this government, by the House of Commons and, of course, by the producers, so that the price of milk in Canada might be raised for the producer.
That of course was reflected by the level of consumption, but it cannot be otherwise. And when the federal government's contribution to this global price amounts to $2.56 of the $10 a hundredweight, I think that this contribution of 25 per cent of the milk price from the federal treasury is very generous, and we have every reason to be proud of it. The $200 million, and even more, that we have distributed directly to the producers from the federal treasury, represented a very fair share, a marked effort and a very positive indication that this government and, namely, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) want to support agriculture in Canada, particularly the dairy industry, because it is a basic product which we could not easily do without. And I think that, as Canadians, we must make all the required efforts to ensure that we shall have enough milk in Canada to meet the needs of all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, this bill gives fairly wide authority to the minister. Of course, I would like to make some suggestions. The minister names some products in the bill, which means that we shall have the assurance that those products will be protected by law. The act gives the definition of the agricultural designated commodities. In subclause
(a)	, there is a list of the products, and subclause (b) reads:
(b)	any other natural or processed product of agriculture... (as defined in the Canadian Wheat Board Act and not marketed through the Canadian Wheat Board) designated by the Governor in Council as an agricultural commodity for the purposes of this Act, hereinafter called "designated commodity";"

Of course.it gives a guarantee for this class of products. But what about the other agricultural commodities? The producers who have those products will have to wait for the goodwill of the government and the minister, for the products to be protected. To receive the protection of the law, they will have no indication a year in advance that their products will be protected at a minimum price.
They will have to wait for the results of a disastrous end of year to make representations to their union or through provincial governments. They will have to have those pressures made on the government in order that their products be considered. And that will inevitably lead to some uncertainty. Mr. Speaker, I would have liked that a few commodities be mentioned in that bill, commodities such as potatoes and maple syrup, which are known and easily identified. Several other commodities could also have been mentioned, and the producers could have been given the guarantee that, should a setback in market prices occur, their revenues would be protected against an overly sharp drop.
That stabilization, Mr. Speaker, and this is not the most appropriate term, is designed to stabilize commodities, both up and down. In other words, it does not freeze a profit to the extend that the latter will not decline; it merely allows a less severe setback of the producer's revenue.
But this will not prevent a setback nor will it prevent or limit an increase. It will, of course, limit a setback but does not impose limits on an increase. That is why in trying to stabilize farm incomes we should ask ourselves if we are doing it at the right time when prices for many commodities are clearly below production costs.
In the last three years production costs for most commodities exceeded the income the producer received on the sale of his products. It is then clear that that five-year average will give a figure clearly below production costs, and I think it is the weakness of our legislation. Will the calculation, the determination of the indexation formula based on the increase in production costs for the five years on which the formula will be based fill that gap? Mr. Speaker, when the minister rises and closes this debate I would like him to explain a bit more clearly how that formula will work because, basically, it is in that formula that really lies the answer to the needs of farmers.
If that formula is not adequate, if it does not give precisely that fair margin of profit to producers as related to their production cost, if it does not properly reflect that increase in production costs in recent years, we are then going to stabilize the floor price for products clearly below the cost of production, and not necessarily have solved the problem. We might have prevented the problem from getting worse, of course, but we will not have necessarily solved the basic problem which is a return on work, investments and production costs, in fact a return on the market to cover costs. That is why I would like the minister to consider seriously adding certain commodities to his bill so they will be covered immediately, and second, I would like him to be more specific on the formula of indexation for those commodities. I spoke of standard farms, Mr. Speaker, and I have spoken of them more than
Agricultural Stabilization Act
once. Those standard farms which already exist to a certain extent in our country, although they have other objectives, could be extended, as far as their concept is concerned, to meet the objective I have mentioned.
Yet, will we succeed in keeping young farmers on the farms? Will we succeed in ensuring that our present farmers will be replaced and will we succeed in drawing other people to agriculture, to ensure Canadians with a sufficient production of food? It is also our duty to those who need it and for whom we are responsible.
We recently passed second reading amendments to the Farm Credit Act which will allow young farmers to get a start. This will help them get established in agriculture. I believe that we have not solved the whole problem, because if they are not given more credit, if fewer investments are required in the first place and if, which seems a good idea, they are allowed to earn some money outside of farming for five years to make their business a bit more profitable, and if we do not grant them a guaranteed income, I am not certain that we shall attract young people to farming, Mr. Speaker.
There is a lot of talk about a guaranteed income for society in general and I believe we should give a lot of thought to establishing a guaranteed income for farmers. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if we should not consider a guaranteed salary for farmers because even if the salary were only basic, even if it were only $50 or $75 a week, I believe that the farmers would at least be ensured of a weekly or monthly minimum income and would have the incentive to work more to improve their farm, their productivity and the general performance of their business. This will probably have to be done, Mr. Speaker. Some may say that this is going very far. We should not be afraid of going that far, Mr. Speaker, if we want to maintain farm production in our country. This may be the price we shall have to pay because I am convinced that, in view of the way things are going in farming, and if we go back to what has been happening during the last ten years, we can predict for the future a situation in which, if we do not guarantee an income for farmers, they will leave their business and we will have great difficulty in making them go back to farming.
Not only will it be difficult to bring people back to farming, but it will cost much more, Mr. Speaker, to reestablish someone who has left farming than it would cost us today to make the necessary efforts to keep him in farming.
We are dealing with a bill whose object is to prevent agriculture from regressing from one year to another. It is a step in the right direction and I thank the minister for it. I hope hon. members, while making constructive criticism, will accept to refer this bill to the committee for a more thorough examination, to enable us to get more information from the minister and his officials so that they may explain to us-I believe they will be able to do so-the mechanisms, the means through which they hope to establish a guaranteed minimum price for farm products, which will be the actual reflection of production costs, and which will thereby guarantee an income to producers and enable them to carry on with their business.
Mr. Speaker, with this I shall conclude and I hope that the other pieces of legislation presented to this House and

March 6, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
related to agriculture will be quickly examined here. If I may do so, I humbly suggest that to hon. members who readily critize the government and the Minister of Agriculture, by saying they are not doing enough for agriculture. I am asking them not to accept without giving their opinion, but to examine the five bills before the House and to strive to have them expedited and passed in committee and brought back to this House for enactment so that we may appeal again to the minister and say that we want more.
Even if we asked the minister to introduce other pieces of legislation to improve agriculture, he will say: Well, pass the one I tabled first and then I will introduce more. I think we could challenge our two ministers who look after agriculture by passing the nine bills before us now. Let us dispose of those nine bills and then let us ask for more. And if they do not introduce any more to improve conditions and to cope with the situation, they will incur all the odium of the situation because they will have to introduce legislation in this House to improve agriculture.
I am not entirely satisfied with the legislation before us, but since it is an important step in the right direction, towards my aim, which I think everyone has, to provide guaranteed farm receipts I therefore recommend that we approve the bill, refer it to the committee and proceed to the consideration of another bill which, of course, seeks price support for western Canada products, grain particularly. It has no positive effect in eastern Canada, but since it is generally in the interest of the Canadian farm industry, I assure the House that we are going to criticize it. I now give notice to the responsible minister. We shall also criticize Bill C-41 a little. That is normal and I guarantee that we shall support the bill because it is for the good of Canadian agriculture.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Assistant Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, someone once said that wisdom is nine parts silence and one part brevity. I will try to be brief in commenting on this bill. It is not a revolutionary or far reaching bill. It will amend the government's stabilization legislation in some ways which have become important. The main features of this bill are these: it changes the list of mandatory products, shortens the base period, increases the guaranteed support level, indexes the guaranteed support price to the level of production costs, and provides for regional support programs.
Shortening the base period from ten to five years is a step in the right direction. But costs have escalated so rapidly that it is possible that by using the average price received in the previous five years the support level will be far below the cost of production. The bill provides for a guarantee of 90 per cent, instead of 80 per cent, of the average price received during the base period. But often this will not be enough. This provision represents a retreat from the way in which base prices for agricultural products were calculated at one time. Because of present inflation rates, a guarantee representing 90 per cent of the average price received in the previous five years may be well below the cost of production. This means that the guarantee means nothing to the farmer except that the support price may be well below his cost of production.

Like the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard), I have some serious reservations about the proposed indexing formula. The minister will need to explain this before the committee or the bill may have to be amended in order that the support which is to be provided when the indexing formula is used can be meaningful, and in order that the guarantee will at least meet the cost of production to the primary producer.
Another feature of the legislation is provision of a regional support program, a program which would have application to a number of provinces but not to the entire country. The minister has referred to this already in reference to a support price for potatoes, suggesting that Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario might be a regional support price area under the amended act. I am not, as yet, convinced that this would be desirable but I am glad to see that the bill will make this kind of set-up possible if it is deemed to be desirable.
For many years parliament has struggled with the question of securing adequate remuneration for farmers. From time to time governments have secured the passage of legislation with high hopes, only to find the results discouraging not only to themselves but to those the legislation was designed to help. Although I do not wish to be unduly pessimistic, I have some reservations about the extent to which this legislation will be effective. I hope the committee, when studying the bill, will look into every aspect closely and hear witnesses with a view to ascertaining the extent to which primary producers will, in fact, benefit from this measure.
The public is inclined to look upon farm legislation and price stabilization measures as having little or nothing to do with the consumer. The usual impression is that they concern only the primary producer. In fact, something like the reverse is actually the case. Bills having to do with the stabilization of farm income have a tremendous implication for consumers. If the market is allowed to operate as it seems to do naturally, failure to take remedial action will have dire consequences for the consumer, because if farmers continue to receive prices which are well below their cost of production it is only a matter of time before they are forced out of business; before they can no longer produce food even though they may desire to continue to do so. The result, in the long run, is a shortage of supply, a shortage which leads to unconscionably high prices necessary to pay for imported food or to lure would-be farmers back into production in the face of high costs involved in redeveloping land.
Part of the difficulty is that the agricultural industry is not very sensitive to the law of supply and demand, especially in this day and age when farmers tend to specialize. It often happens that a farmer cannot readily cut down his production if the price is not right. He does not withhold his product from the market when prices are falling, in line with the classic economic theory of what should happen. This is not what happens, particularly when the goods are perishable. As a matter of fact, the process seems to run in the opposite direction: as the farmer's margin of profit decreases, he is forced to produce more simply in order to live and pay his overhead charges. He struggles to produce more and more just in order to
March 6, 1975

keep his head above water, until the point is reached at which there is no profit margin and the market is flooded, at which time a large number of farmers are forced out of business through bankruptcy. This is not a situation which affords any satisfaction to consumers.
The objective of a bill as the one before us should be to provide a fair return to a farmer for his labour and his investment, at least with respect to part of his production-he can perhaps gamble on the remainder. This involves the establishment of a base price at least for a quota of his production, a base price which is realistically tied to the cost of production. As I have already remarked, there is very little relationship between present-day costs of production and average prices for the last five or ten years. In these circumstances, it behooves the minister to explain how the formula proposed in the bill will bring about a sound relationship between the cost of production and the base price proposed. The cost of production should make provision for at least a living wage for primary producers; what would be looked upon as a minimum wage in other industries.
There is a wider benefit which a bill such as this should strive to attain. Not only should it seek to help primary producers as individuals but it should be aimed at helping to preserve a rural society in this country. It was recognized in pioneer days, and I hope it is recognized still, that rural Canada has made an extremely important contribution to this country in non-economic ways, that is to say, in social ways. It gives the country stability and provides an environment in which a fine type of life-I would say the finest type of life-can be lived. It helps maintain an environment which produces a quality of life not obtainable in the cities in this technological age, or if it is obtainable there it can be achieved only at an almost prohibitive cost.
Therefore, I think it is in the long-range interest of this country as a whole to look upon the primary producers not as mere automatons or units of statistics producing cheap food for the people who really count-presumably people in urban areas. We should take a much more enlightened overview of the situation and recognize that people in rural areas are in themselves important. They are a very necessary segment of society who live in an environment that has the potential for producing the best quality of life that can be achieved in this country.
This is especially so in modern times where technology has made it possible for someone living in the country to have, as it were, the best of both worlds. He can have the benefits of modern living, on the one hand-provided he has the minimum income required-and, on the other hand, he can enjoy the many benefits of country life, where he can experience the beneficial effects of being close to nature, the opportunity of solitude now and again, and obtain an in-focus view of the place of humanity in the whole nature of things. This helps one realize that human beings are part of a very much larger web of life, and if we forget this elementary fact it will not bode well for our future as a country.
Some years ago I remember as a child seeing old coins which were minted over 100 years ago with a slogan on
Agricultural Stabilization Act
them. They depicted a sheaf of wheat on the one side, a plow on the other, and the slogan was "Speed the plow". This use of the word "speed" in its archaic sense means "prosper the plow", such as you would speed a parting guest. In those days they recognized that the basic health of the nation depended to a great extent on the economic health of rural Canada.
I hold the view that this philosophy is still valid and that we cannot have a healthy country as a whole without making certain that we have a healthy rural segment in society. I might say, in connection with the motto "Speed the plow", that there is an old English song that expresses a point of view that has gone out of fashion, one that even country people are loth to express and which I am sure the average statistical planner hidden away in some bureaucracy thinks is old-fashioned and no longer valid. I should like to quote a line or two of it:
I have lawns, I have bowers,
I have fruit, I have flowers,
The lark is my morning alarmer.
So, jolly boys, now
Here's God speed the plough
Long life and success to the farmer.
I think the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has a great responsibility-and not only the present minister but any minister of agriculture-to do his best, in co-operation with his counterparts in the provinces, to make sure everything reasonable is done to provide an adequate economic base for the primary producer so he can stay in production and benefit not only himself and the country as a whole but Canadian consumers of food over the long term, and this includes every member of society in Canada.
In closing, I want to bring to the minister's attention the alarming situation existing in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick at the present time in regard to potato production. These amendments to the act will not do anything in time to save the situation for the potato producers in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick who are subsidizing the consumers of their product to an alarming extent. I do not think the consumers of potatoes would begrudge the price they would have to pay so long as the primary producer received a fair price. But the irony is that everyone who handles potatoes from the time they are produced until they find their way to grocers' shelves is probably making just as much profit in a poor year as they would in a year when potatoes are reasonably well priced. The same amount of freight is paid on potatoes, there is the same mark-up in the stores, and the jobbers take the same percentage. Those who supply containers make the same profit as in any other year. But the primary producer has to suffer a loss when the consumer does not pay a reasonable price for his product.
I should like to see action taken to correct this situation in the long run. In the meanwhile, I implore the minister to implement as quickly as possible some emergency plan, if he has not already done so, to divert present production in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick to some other use or to export-subsidies would be required-so that this year the producers will not be pushed into bankruptcy and will be able to plant a crop this spring. This

March 6, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
emergency action should be taken so they can continue to produce what is one of the best food values the Canadian consumer can have, even when the price is a profitable one for the primary producer.

speechtext:
Yet another part of the legislation which is very open to discussion and question is that part regarding the participation of producers and/or provinces to set a higher support price than that provided under the law. It seems to me that present legislation already provides for a base level but not an upper limit. One could facetiously argue that the minister put that clause in the bill with the intention of setting a support price somewhat lower than adequate and then saying to the producers and provinces, "Either put up or shut up".
I	said at the outset that I did not intend to take up too much time of the House on this topic, important though it is, so let me conclude by saying that I support the minister's idea of making Canada self-sufficient in terms of agriculture. Nevertheless, if we are to achieve this goal we must strive to help the farmer keep his self-respect in terms of the arduous task he is performing. As I said earlier, it is not enough to extol the virtues of the farming community; farmers are sick and tired of this. At a time when millions are going hungry around the world, we must cease treating farmers as third-class citizens. Farmers are becoming a rarity in communities right across the country. Let us provide them with the respect they rightly deserve. The means of achieving this is to provide them with reasonable stability as far as marketing procedures are concerned. If this government and the minister continue to pursue the type of ad hoc policies they have pursued in the past, we will only be pushing more individuals out of a field which is vital to both Canada and the world.
In a speech to a Lion's club on February 18, 1975, the minister stated:
-farmers despise subsidies; they would rather get a fair income out of the marketplace-
I agree to an extent, but let me read what the minister stated on another occasion:
When land is frozen into farming, farmers have no choice-at that point it is society's responsibility, his and mine, to provide the climate that will give an efficient farmer a reasonable return.
Let the minister act on his own words. If I understand the farming community accurately, what farmers want and desperately need is the assurance that when they raise a herd or plant a crop they will have a fairly good idea of what they will get in the way of prices when they market their products. To the best of my knowledge, 2,000 industrial milk producers in Ontario, and 2,600 in the province of Quebec, gave up and sold out in 1973 because they simply could not get a decent price. I see the minister shaking his head. This may have been in 1972, but it was certainly in the last two or three years. This tragedy must come to an end: I think the minister would agree with that. We just cannot continue to take farmers for granted in this callous fashion.
The welfare of this country still depends on the top six or eight inches of its arable land-land which is, incidentally, shrinking in acreage all the time because it is being sold for urban and industrial development. This is a problem with which the Minister of Agriculture or somebody in the federal government must come to grips. We should pass very strong federal laws to restrict the growth of cities and urban communities in those areas of Canada where there is valuable arable land. This is not being done. Local municipalities, township councils, and so on, are
Agricultural Stabilization Act
attempting to do it but they do not have the clout of the federal government: only the federal government can do this, and it should do it very quickly. Unless the minister moves more quickly, we will end up being a net importer.
As an indication of how fed-up the farmers are becoming, one need only read some of the current speeches made by the president of the Federation of Agriculture, which for years was simply an offshoot of the Ontario Progressive Conservative Party. The speeches Mr. Hill has been making recently remind me of the speeches representatives of the Farmers' Union were making ten years ago. That is how desperate many small and large "C" conservative farmers are today in Ontario, where he is calling for very stringent bargaining powers. His speeches almost read like trade unionist speeches. That is where they are going at the present time: I look forward to the time when the farmer recognizes he has a friend in the trade union movement and when the trade union movement recognizes it has a friend in the farmer. Both must bargain for wages and prices.
If the minister, his predecessor and the government were more responsible in respect of the farmer, they would have done something and this situation would not have come about. However, today the farmer is becoming angry: this is evident in my constituency when I am invited to the many rural dances, banquets, and so on. The warden's banquet is one of the biggest. While the farmers, when they attend, are not angry and do not intend to embarrass me, at these social functions I receive a very distinct impression that they are very unhappy and that something is wrong in the rural community today.
In closing, I suggest that while the Minister of Agriculture does much travelling and makes speeches to many farm groups and individual farmers, he should stop talking and start looking. In that way my waste-paper basket would not be so full, and he might learn something from the farmers.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity this afternoon to add any support to the bill before us. Because of involvement in agriculture and the diversified area I represent, I am sure this bill will add stabilization and confidence to the agricultural industry which is of the utmost importance not only to this country but indeed to the whole world.
I very much appreciate the fact that members on the opposite side of the House have made only token efforts to criticize the bill. I believe they recognize the value of stability and the insurance it gives the agricultural community. Agriculture is, always has been and always will be, the most important industry in this country and indeed in the world, especially today when we recognize the many developing countries and the food shortages which exist. Canada will increase, and has increased, its production of agricultural commodities. It has taken its place in the world and has supported those in need.
In the past we have had haphazard, "dog eat dog" marketing which has not worked out too well. This situation forced many young people to leave the farm and go to

March 6, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
urban areas. The introduction of marketing boards in respect of various commodities has created some stability in the agricultural industry and has encouraged young farmers to remain on the farm. We now have many aggressive and forthright farmers who are eager and willing to put in a day's work to produce our products. Greater efficiency through mechanization of the industry has increased production and has assured a high level of return to the farmer.
I represent a very diversified riding. In fact, it is one of the most productive ridings in Canada. It is sometimes referred to as the Garden of Eden in the Niagara peninsula. We even produce some eggs. In the Niagara peninsula the growing of grapes is one of our major industries. We also produce peaches, pears, cherries, plums and apples. We grow every kind of fruit that it is possible to grow in Canada. We have large areas devoted to vegetable production and the operation of greenhouses. We also have some of the largest poultry operations to be found anywhere in Ontario. In addition, we have some of the largest hog operations to be found anywhere in Ontario, even with all the problems relating to hog operations.
We have many dairy and beef operations in the southern part of the riding. Grains are grown, on a smaller scale, in the southern part of my riding. There is a large horticultural station located in the heart of the riding. Any problems which may exist in respect of agriculture would immediately be found in this particular area. These problems have shown up in the past. Farmers, through their ingenuity and hard work, have overcome many of the problems. However, that is not sufficient; we need some consideration and protection by the higher levels of government.
Contrary to what some people believe, and contrary to what is often reported in the news media, the food industry in my particular area is far from dead or dying. The fruit industry is growing. It is an important industry in this country. In fact, the industry is just getting its second wind through the help of federal government programs. We have assistance at the present time in respect of cold storage facilities. There has been reconsideration of some of the tariff agreements in order to protect our industry and to provide some stability in our markets. The federal government has embarked upon a program which will ensure an adequate supply of labour: our industry sometimes has been hurt because of an inadequate supply.
Now the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is presenting Bill C-50, which is flexible enough to ensure at least some degree of stability in the agricultural field. Certainly there are some weaknesses in the bill. These have been indicated by the opposition members. Nothing is perfect. There is still much to be done to put together a bill which the agricultural people deserve, and we have always taken up this challenge. I believe this is as it should be. This is what has brought about the fact that we have one of the best agricultural industries in the world- one of the most efficient and productive industries. I know, from speaking to many farmers in my area, how they feel about the fact that we have a Minister of Agriculture who knows the problems of our industry, who understands them and who takes action such as is proposed in Bill C-50.

I can go on and on giving examples of the actions of the minister and some of the comments and feedback from the agricultural people in my area. The minister has created, with his presence alone, an air of confidence and stability.

speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of all studies, notes, position papers, memoranda, etc., relating to the requirements of Canadian shipping with respect to the proposed formula for import/ export conference rated seaborne trade, in terms of the number of ships required, the capacity of Canadian shipyards, the number of Canadian merchant seamen required, the level of ancillary shipyard related industries of design capability, etc., in the event Canada ratifies the proposed code of conduct for liner conferences.
