He said: Mr. Speaker, because I have only 20 minutes to speak, I ask the indulgence of the House to allow me to refer to notes so that I will not get sidetracked, because I feel that what we are dealing with is very important. On a very careful reading of Hansard of January 29 and February 12 I am, frankly, at a loss as to why the government wishes to have this motion withdrawn. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mclsaac) is recorded as having said on January 29, at page 2716 of Hansard:
-studies have not been prepared on the hypothetical ramifications of the proposed cargo sharing formula for Canadian ships, shipyards, shipyard related activities, or merchant seamen.
If such is the case, I would submit that it is further concrete evidence of the bumbling incompetence and missed opportunities which have for so long characterized so much of Canada's approach to maritime policy under this government. But to refuse to study the impact of a proposal which could provide Canadian shipyards with over $1 billion of orders, give over 180 new ships a Canadian flag, provide jobs for 7,200 mariners and support an annual payroll of over $150 million, not to mention reduce greatly the estimated $l'/2 billion Canada wastes each year in foreign shipping charges because this administration does not want a Canadian flag fleet for international trade-the reason for that refusal escapes me completely. I noted with confusion that, contrary to what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport said, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Guay) on February 24, at page 3528 of Hansard, said:
At the present time Canada is considering certain factors which will determine whether or not Canada accedes to the code.
In simple terms, I have asked for copies of these studies Canada is making. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport says that no such studies have taken place and asks that I stop requesting them. On the other hand, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion says that Canada is studying the matter. This is obviously a case where the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. When it affects a multibillion dollar industry such as the shipping industry in Canada, it is nothing short of a national disgrace.
On February 24 I complained that a number of questions which had been standing on the order paper for some three months had not been answered. Miraculously, they were answered last Monday. Permit me to read into the record question No. 1131 as follows:
How many ships would be required to accommodate the movement (a) out of Canadian ports to foreign destinations (b) into Canadian ports from foreign destinations of 40 per cent of the present liner conference rated cargo?
I asked this question because the ratification by Canada and sufficient other shipping nations of the proposed code of conduct for liner conferences under discussion today would guarantee Canada an immediate ability to insist on having up to 40 per cent of the present conference rated cargo in and out of Canada. I asked it because at present we have a fraction of 1 per cent carried in Canadian bottoms. I asked it because I was concerned about the impact on Canada, in terms of positive value to the ship-

ping industry, which this code could bring about. What was the answer? It was as follows:
Under section 12 of the Shipping Conferences Exemption Act the Minister of Transport reports annually to parliament on liner conference operations. The latest report covered the calendar year 1973 and was tabled March 28, 1974. ... As indicated in that report statistics collected demonstrated the necessity for closer control at the reporting source and for a refinement of interpretation. Appropriate means of satisfying these requirements are being developed with the co-operation of Statistics Canada. In the meantime, satisfactory statistics are not available on the liner conference rated cargo carried in conference vessels.
In a nutshell, the government does not know what the impact of this proposed code of conduct would be, and that is why I raise the matter. Question No. 1,132, also, after sitting without an answer for three months, received a very hasty answer on Monday. The question was:
How many merchant seamen would be required to accommodate the staffing of the number of ships required to accommodate the movement (a) out of Canadian ports to foreign destinations (b) into Canadian ports from foreign destinations of 40 per cent of the present liner conference rated cargo?
What was the answer? It was:
Satisfactory statistics are not available on the liner conference rated cargo carried in conference vessels.
The government, with some $30 billion to allocate to the priorities of the nation, with hundreds of experts, consultants, advisers, research teams and committees, just plain does not know. I suggest that the government does not know because it does not care. I submit that the Canadian shipbuilding industry, the repair industry, the merchant seamen and all the other maritime related groups in Canada who have given their support so many times to this government have been duped into accepting promises heaped upon promises. There have been pledges heaped upon pledges, behind which there is neither conviction, leadership, dedication nor coherent, philosophical attachment.
It is instructive to ask why this lamentable situation exists. Howard Darling, in his scholarly report entitled "The elements of an international shipping policy for Canada" released by the government on January 30 this year, condemns the lack of any single, identifiable department responsible for Canadian maritime policy. He points out that the present statutory provisions relating to shipping in the National Transportation Act are hangovers from 1947 when we had a fleet. We do not have one now, yet the law remains unchanged since then. There is no cabinet or executive directive to fill this incredible legislative void. As of January 30, 1975, all we have is an interdepartmental committee, lacking cabinet direction and lacking a mandate from anyone but the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand).
More incredibly, prior to January 30, 1975, we did not have so much as an interdepartmental committee. Does this indicate high level concern? Who is responsible? Is it the Department of Transport, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, or the Department of External Affairs? I was even more confused when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion took the ball for the government in the debate of February 24.
March 6, 1975

Let us travel a bit farther down the road. The Minister of Transport has been on record for over 30 years as being in favour of some form of merchant marine in Canada, first with the CNTU and most recently as Minister of Transport. On November 4, 1974, at page 1007 of Hansard, he is recorded as being in favour of this. In answer to a question I raised with him as to whether Canada would accede to the proposed code of conduct for liner conferences, he said:
I am inclined to support the idea which the hon. member expressed, that he is in favour of a merchant marine in Canada.
Naturally enough, the newspapers across Canada for the umpteenth time reported that the government was inclined to support or favour a merchant marine: something of a fraud, I suggest. The same minister today says to this House that he has not studied the matter and asks that members of parliament not ask questions or seek information, and he asks me to withdraw a motion calling upon the government to put up or shut up. I submit that the government indeed has some shadowy studies, but because of its all too characteristic tendency to sleepwalk and evade issues and answers it has not given any priority to the matter. The same government which spends thousands of dollars researching the origin of the term "fuddle-duddle", today says that it cannot find the money, the men or the will to study the impact on Canada of its dependence upon foreign flag fleets to carry Canada's export trade.
Mr. Speaker, I find that argument incredible, and indeed somewhat repugnant. It is arrogance untrammelled. It is carelessness reduced to its purest form. I reject it and feel confident that if government members opposite, particularly those from areas where shipbuilding is important, such as Saint John, New Brunswick, and the St. Lawrence River valley in Quebec, really took the time to do some work, to have a look, to do other than applaud the endless stream of meaningless and diversionary press releases and rhetoric emanating from every orifice of this administration, they would be shocked and would cry out for remedial action to end what is surely one of the nation's greatest embarrassments.
[DOT] <mo)
The government says it has not even the ability to find the basic figures, and after almost a year has elapsed since this agreement was signed at Geneva by an overwhelming majority of the nations represented at UNCTAD it says that it does not know and it does not want to know. Mr. Speaker, the government has derided the efforts of members on this side of the House in the past. It said that we were misguided and wrong when we called out unanimously for a "Canadian only" coasting trade. It said we were ill-advised, that we would offend our rich and powerful friends, that we did not have the yard capacity, that we did not have the men.
After three years of hounding, and after the foreign fleets swelled their numbers in our coasting trade, they finally acted. Slowly, painfully and with incredible reluctance, this government was forced, by arguments of sheer economics and pressing national interest, to move; and they moved to admit that they had been wrong and that they had sought poor counsel. Mr. Speaker, this raises a
Shipping
crucial point. The government, when faced with the recommendations of Howard Darling with respect to a Canadian coasting fleet, first sought advice from the industry. This was a natural step. But in doing so, the government failed to appreciate the fact that the shipping industry that serves Canada is essentially non-Canadian. It is predictable that the agents in Canada of the foreign shipping cartels would be opposed to any expansion of new Canadian vessels into their territory.
The government first listened to these people and said no. Later, on the advice of their own transportation specialists who were detached, responsible and concerned with serving Canadian interests rather than the interests of New York, Tokyo, Athens and London, the light became more clear and eventually I was pleased to see the government act in the genuine interests of Canada.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the government is here again to say to us that it has not studied the matter, that it has not sought the documented advice of its own professional civil servants; to say that it is prepared to accept without question the opinions of the Canadian chamber of shipping, the Canadian shipping federation and others who represent in Canada a by and large foreign interest. I am prepared to give odds to anyone of 100 to 1 that if these interests are relied upon, their reaction will be, "Where is the cancer?" or, "We serve Canada well. Why change a good thing?"
Mr. Speaker, doing nothing is always easy, but Canada surely ought not to be seeking simply the easy way. It ought to be seeking to identify the Canadian national interest and then seeking to identify the ways and means by which this interest can best be served. To rely exclusively upon historically unreliable advice, to deny our public servants a chance to look into the matter from the Canadian point of view, is not only dishonest but potentially catastrophic. The reasons for this are many. Canada, it is estimated, loses in excess of $114 billion every year in shipping charges paid to foreign shipping concerns to transport our goods to foreign markets and to bring into Canada those things we purchase abroad-$114 billion every year! Mr. Speaker, this is a staggering sum, a sum which is an enormous drain on our foreign exchange resources.
If hon. members opposite would take the time to do other than pat themselves on the back and applaud the endless drivel coming from the treasury benches, they would see that I have asked on the order paper for confirmation of this figure. I know that for years many others have sought from the government their estimate of this figure, without success. This is another example of the overriding fact that this government does not know and seems not to care. A figure that was churned out on Monday, after the government had grunted and groaned for three months, indicated that in 1972 the nationality of registry of the vessels serving Canada under liner conference arrangements referred to and overseen in a typically inadequate manner by the Canadian Transport Commission, pursuant to the Shipping Conferences Exemption Act-an act which, incidentally, gives these liner conference groupings the right to price-fix, rate-fix and act totally outside the scope of Canada's combines legislation-was as follows: Great Britain, 52; Norway, 48; Japan,

Shipping
31; United States, 29; Liberia, 19; Italy, 16; Sweden, 11; Greece, 9; France, 4; others, 233.
For the skeptical, the cynical and for the interest of those who in fact have some concern in this regard, this answer is found on page 3702 of Hansard. But here is the crunch: how many ships of this total involved in the liner conference trade to and from Canada were of Canadian registry? There was, Mr. Speaker, not a single, solitary one. Nil. Not one. Of the 452 ships that served Canada in these conferences, not one was registered in Canada. And the government comes to this chamber today to say that it does not feel that the proposed code of conduct for liner conferences drawn up by the overwhelming majority of the world's shipping countries ought to be studied.
The government says that the code is hypothetical, that it is not really of concern to us, that the Government of Canada is prepared to accept without so much as a second look the irresponsible opinions of the agents of the foreign shipping cartels, that members of parliament ought not even to ask the general question, that government has the whole situation under control. This is a disgrace, a disgrace born of neglect and fostered in an atmosphere of hypocrisy and near deceit. This government stands condemned if it persists in operating under the unseemly and all too cosy influence of the foreign shipping cartels. There is no doubt that its present attitude is identical to that of these offshore interests, and there is no evidence today that it is about to change its direction.
I can safely predict that there will follow in this chamber a great gush of words and sympathy. They will applaud their efforts, they will cheer their direction. But if that is the case, Mr. Speaker, the cheers will be hollow, having been spawned in deceit and nourished by years of neglect. Not a single Canadian ship is involved in the liner conference trade serving Canada. Surely no Canadian spokesman can cheer this disgraceful situation. That is all I am after today. I, alone, cannot change the course of events affecting Canada's so-called maritime policy. But I am convinced that this government can, and indeed that this government must.
Permit me to cite another factor. International inflation has resulted in a tremendous increase in the cost of building and operating large fleets of ships to serve the international seaborne trade so crucial to the development of the world community. This has resulted in a drastic reduction of the number of companies involved in the ownership and operation of ships. The mergers, conglomerations, takeovers and the like in the world shipowning community have been remarkable.
At the same time, in the last 20 years governments all over the world have begun to take a second look at their subsidization policies. Where they once simply shelled out the money, now they are saying, "Here is the money you need, but we want four seats on your board of directors; we want a percentage of your voting stock; we want to be involved with the direction in which you place your lines; we want to ensure that if public, national money is put into your operation, it operates in the interests of the home country, that it does what it is told and that it is an active arm of our foreign policy, a tool for our national purpose." That is what foreign countries are saying to their shipping companies today.

It is the increasing participation by foreign governments in the direction of the foreign fleets presently serving Canada that poses, according to Howard Darling, the greatest threat to Canada's national interests. As the response I have cited demonstrates, Canada has no capability to move her vital export trade nor her crucial import trade except in foreign bottoms. These foreign bottoms increasingly are committed to serve the expressed national and foreign policies of members of the world community other than Canada. This is an unhealthy dependence, a dependence that is fraught with real and possible difficulties for Canada, and a policy that ought not to be pursued by this government nor tolerated by this parliament.
The UNCTAD proposals would seek to ensure that Canada could insist that up to 40 per cent of our import and export trade carried by liner conferences be carried in Canadian bottoms, yet this government does not want so much as to study the proposal. It seeks today to have the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada consent to a policy of "no Canadian involvement in the liner conferences" and to agree that what we are doing is all well and good. Members of this party will not accept that all is well. They will not accept that the sleepwalking and lack of direction so far demonstrated is good enough because, simply put, it is not. Forty per cent of the present trade, as opposed to nil per cent: if the figure given of 452 ships is accurate, 40 per cent would be 180 ships, as opposed to none at all.
Let us pursue the implications for Canada of ratification and implementation of the proposed cargo sharing formula enunciated in the UNCTAD agreement. If Canada insisted on a full 40 per cent of the bottoms, at about 40 men per ship the total jobs created would be approximately 7,200. That would be increased to almost 10,000, given the cycling of men on and off duty. At the present rates of pay for mariners, the payroll would be close to $150 million-a lot of money. If the average cost of an SD 14 dry cargo carrier, with a capacity for 14,000 tons of cargo is $8 million, an order for 180 ships would mean, for Canadian yards, more than $1.5 billion. This is the promise of the concept behind UNCTAD.
Add it up, Mr. Speaker. Annual losses of $1.5 billion in foreign exchange; orders for Canadian shipyards of more than $1.5 billion; an annual payroll for Canadian mariners of $150 million. And this government refuses to look at the matter, refuses to even study it. Canadian export and import of goods is under attack. UNCTAD serves as a warning. We would be fools to ignore it. I urge the Government of Canada to reverse its present attitude of "It's all right, Jack" and initiate action now and for the future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raynald Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member who has made such a clear exposition of the whole merchant marine, coastal shipping and shipbuilding issue in Canada.
If there is someone here who is really interested in this issue as the elected representative of a riding with a shipbuilding industry, it is the hon. member for Levis. And I did not wait until I was elected to the House of

Commons to talk about a merchant marine in Canada. I used to talk about it when I was chairman of the Lauzon Board of Trade. I am known in my riding as the merchant marine Member of Parliament, and I feel this is a much more worthy title to fame than ending up like the hon. member for Darmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) who has produced a mountain of papers to establish the necessity of a merchant marine. I shall try to do it in the few minutes at my disposal. This afternoon, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East did not need in fact a mountain of reports, studies and principles to state his views not only on the code of ethic, but also on the creation of a merchant marine for Canada.
He criticized earlier a statement made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion who answered a question on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). I must quote in full that answer, and I wonder if one should quote out of context a statement that lasted three minutes. He seemed to criticize this statement which I quote:
I believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is on record as being inclined to support the idea of a Canadian merchant fleet. The circumstances which dictated Canada's abandoning its merchant marine fleet after the Second World War have changed greatly. The convention promotes national shipping lines, but the definition embraces even foreign ships under charter. Hence, accession to the convention would not in itself imply any commitment to develop a merchant marine.
But having personally followed the Minister of Transport in the Province of Quebec and everywhere across this country, I think that reference should not be made only to part of the answer. For my part, I did not wait to be here in this House of Commons to talk about a merchant fleet to prove my sincerity. When I participated in debates on a merchant fleet, it was not to go and get some votes but to think also about the statements by which the Minister of Transport has always stood.
When he was president of the CNTU-the central council-the minister demanded, and I congratulate him for doing so, in co-operation with several departments, that consideration be given to setting up a merchant fleet. Indeed he and his predecessors are the ones who took the decision. Mr. Speaker, if we want to talk about a merchant fleet I think we must do it by steps. What do we want in the end? How are we to proceed? The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East said earlier that we have had enough studies, enough reports, that we need action.
But why in a notice of motion for production of papers does he ask that all those papers be tabled in the House? I have before me, Mr. Speaker, 8, 10 or 12 reports on coastal shipping, a merchant fleet, on the code of ethics, and I would like to sum up very quickly the two main reports.
I think that if we want precisely to build a merchant fleet we must do it by steps.
We saw that in 1971, the government, through the former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, stated in this House that before thinking of building a Canadian merchant navy, subsidy and support programs are needed in order to help us modernize our shipyards and make them more efficient and more productive.
Shipping
It is the STAP program, as we like to call it and I even know that some hon. members this afternoon in this House seem to entertain doubts about the efficiency of this program. I have not heard, fortunately, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) criticize the program. If we consider its efficiency, we saw that from 1971 until 1973, subsidies amounting to 14 and 17 percent of the cost of vessels were granted under the program in order to help shipyards become competitive on the world market.
That's to look after our friends off-shore. But what about Canadians?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall come back to the comments of the hon. member who spoke before me.
I would like to tell him that I have listened with great attention to his comments and that what I have to say, when I have finished, will probably interest him. I hope he will give me his support in the fight that I have made until now, even if I am on the side of the government, so that Canada may have a merchant marine.
Indeed, motion No. 50 asks the government to consider reviving the Canadian merchant marine and applying the recommendations of the Darling report. I hope the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East will not only support me during the debate on this motion, but will also try to influence his party, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is doing, about the position to take concerning the motion I have made in this House.
I have been told that I was being somewhat revolutionary. I am not a revolutionary, Mr. Speaker, I am simply a member of Parliament who has the right to speak, even though I am on the side of the government. And I ask the hon. member, as well as those of the Social Credit and the New Democratic Party, to give priority to this motion, not only to know if we must produce reports, policy statements or other material, but to study this issue immediately. As I ask in this motion, I would like the immediate establishment of a merchant marine in Canada to be considered. On this point, I am in agreement with the Minister of Transport because it is better for us. If we follow the whole process up till now, we see very clearly that only one step remains, and this does not involve the production of a report or papers.
We must merely see to it that an agency or a department-as I myself asked the House in November when I took part in the debate on the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner)-studies the possibility of creating a department or an agency entrusted with making all decisions and getting laws enacted.
I had the opportunity of rising in the House yesterday and stating that I was speaking on behalf of the shipyard workers; after all that is an industry, and the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East knows it as well as I do. That industry is truly essential in Canada, not only to provide jobs indirectly, but to provide them directly to some 18,500 workers as a means of livelihood.
We will also have an opportunity to find out, through an analysis of that program, whether-as was implied yester-

Mr. Speaker, the announcement also mentions a partial cut in the subsidy. I also was somewhat disappointed at first, because the industries had grown accustomed to getting 17 per cent. But a stop has been put to that, which is the very proof that control is to be exercized on the use of subsidies. It has been stated that if the company invests 3 per cent, the government also commits itself to investing 3 per cent, to better help the industry to modernize and become more productive and more efficient, in order that when the last step has been made in the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine, those ships will be built here. I think it would have been hardly advisable, ten or fifteen years ago, to say in this House: We are going to build a merchant marine. It was not easy, Mr. Speaker, because our shipyards could not do the job at that time. We had to do it progressively.
Mr. Speaker, the STAP program, and I shall conclude on this, was good. It was good to repeat the purpose of that program in this House. No direct criticism was made, only veiled charges. Not even an hour ago, Mr. Speaker, I was talking with shipbuilders. I am not saying they are fully satisfied, no, because there was a degradation in that program. I shall have the opportunity of discussing and criticizing that program if necessary later in this House, but we must nevertheless commend the government for that step forward. I am glad to see that some members of the opposition seem to support what I am saying this afternoon in the House.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a scheme to distribute gifts and in concluding I will say that STAP is not imbued with favouritism. The program was carried out from 1971 to 1974 in 14 Canadian shipyards and we know that there are some 40 or 50 shipyards of various sizes in the country.
It has been stated that this could help the companies where investigations are launched, but I do not want to discuss the matter, Mr. Speaker. However, when such things are insinuated, I say that one must be unbiased. When the question was asked this afternoon to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, he answered that the dredging operations were under investigation. Does the member for Darmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) specifically want to help us create a merchant marine? Without that program, Mr. Speaker, our shipyards would be entirely unable to undertake their own modernization.

Several reports have been mentioned. People apparently believe that we remain idle. The Darling report was published in October 1970, Mr. Speaker and I entirely agree with the previous speaker about it.
What were the main recommendations? I think it is worth looking at what happened after those reports were released, and I will do it very rapidly. Of the main recommendations, the first was:
1.	The Canadian coasting trade should be reserved to Canadian-flag
vessels.
2.	Exploitation of Arctic and continental shelf resources should be done according to standards governing the extent of use of Canadian shipping to be required.
And I think, Mr. Speaker, that is about what the hon. member who spoke before me said, asking how many vessels were involved. It is attested by his motion. And it is found in the first Darling report on coasting trade. The third recommendation is:
3.	The policy of issuing permits should be directed as much as possible and practicable toward replacing foreign vessels by Canadian vessels ... Permits should be issued to non-Canadian flag vessels only if Canadian vessels are either unavailable, insufficient or inadequate for the purpose.
4.	The provisions regarding the reservation of the coasting trade to Canadian-flag vessels should extend to the other marine activities of dredging, salvage, seismographic, supply and support vessels in offshore drilling.
5.	Government assistance to new marine industries should have attached conditions on the extend of use of Canadian shipping to be required.
And that is exactly what has been done, Mr. Speaker, I refer to the Minister of External Affairs and the Minister of Transport, who made a statement, on May 23, 1974. We have published it. I see that the hon. member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) has the paper. For his benefit, I quote:
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Jean Marchand) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mitchell Sharp) have jointly announced today that Canada will not abide anymore by some provisions of the British Commonwealth Merchant Agreement of 1931, as it was announced last fall, and consequently will reserve coastal trade in Canada to Canadian-flag vessels. A one year's notice to that effect is then given to the other member countries.
Mr. Speaker, if we are told that nothing has been done right then, if we read the first sub-section-I see that my time flies away very fast, and I would not like to forget anything-we can see that it was a first step. There was the STAP Program; there is this very firm statement of the minister. In co-operation with the Minister for External Affairs, we have made another step forward. Do we need so many documents for the third step? I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that so many documents are required to know that the country, the government of Canada has arrived at a no-return point.
In concluding my remarks, I will take the liberty to quote the Darling Report which has been released recently by Mr. Darling himself and which is meant to be a constructive approach. I will merely give a very short summary of the studies made by Mr. Darling on the matter of a merchant fleet in Canada and on how one is to be built.
I fully agree with him. In fact, I have had the opportunity to say so not only in the House, but outside, on TV, on

the air and through the other media. The first criticism that the Darling Report expresses is the following: We have no legislation whatsoever concerning the creation of a merchant fleet in Canada. We have no well defined policy. We have no administrative guidelines.
I had not read the criticism in the Darling report. I trust the opposition will not consider my criticism as negative, but on the contrary as positive. I had the opportunity to say in this House that it will be necessary to create either a department or a body within which we may more readily establish priorities for the immediate future and no longer on the long term basis, to create a Canadian merchant navy.
Mr. Speaker, as it is stated in the Darling Report, I believe we have no definite goal. Since the Darling report says so ... I come to conclusions. I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are getting impatient, you want me to conclude my remarks on this major and urgent problem for the benefit and the prestige of the Canadian nation. As I said before on many occasions, our country is the one that has the longest coast line. We have a large river, we have the Arctic but we have no merchant marine. This is really pitiful.
And now, Mr. Speaker, on to the Darling report recommendations. We shall need a more positive attitude toward problems inherent in the establishment of a merchant marine. Greater authority will also be needed to set these priorities within a sole department. In fact, decisions are now taken either by the Department of Transport, by the Department of Industry and Trade and Commerce or by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen). Tasks are being shared and we work a little in a slapdash way. But should the government want-

Shipping

Perhaps you will allow me to read into the record some statistics drawn from official government sources, namely, the former Canadian Maritime Commission, on the Canadian dry cargo merchant fleet. This gives the number of ships that there were in this fleet from 1948 to 1972. In 1948 Canada had 203 dry cargo merchant vessels of 10,000 tons. Ten years later, in 1958, Canada had three dry cargo merchant vessels of 10,000 tons, and two dry cargo merchant vessels of 3,000 tons, for a total of five. In 10 years our merchant marine had withered away from 203 to five.
In 1968, 10 years later, Canada had two dry cargo merchant vessels of 30,000 tons and one dry cargo merchant vessel of 10,000 tons. The two 30,000-tonners had been launched in 1964 and 1968 after a program of assistance to shipbuilding was introduced by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). By 1972, and this remains true today, Canada had lost the entire fleet it had in 1968.
I am delighted that the hon. member for Levis is so enthusiastically in support of shipbuilding, and I know why. The reason is that this affects his riding. For the same reason I am enthusiastically in support of the shipbuilding industry. Through the hon. member for Levis I hope this message gets to the government, namely, that the activities of the government have caused this deplorable situation to develop.
Yesterday there was distributed to the press and to my office over in the Confederation Building, so I did not find it until I got there this morning, having been busy in committees the rest of the day, a press release on shipbuilding. I welcome it with certain reservations, because altogether too much of the subsidies is going to the riding of the hon. member for Levis and not nearly enough to my own riding. I hope you will permit that reservation, which I think is understandable.
As a result of the activities of the government the shipbuilding capacity in my riding has deteriorated to the point where it is practically non-existent. This is absolutely deplorable, and I would invite the hon. member to come out and see its sad state. It is his government that is responsible. Now we have this half measure involving a 17 per cent assistance program.
This need for a merchant marine, and for other types of ships built in Canada, is becoming more and more important, and we have witnessed this increasing importance in the last 10 years. We have just seen a saga develop in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Had it not such serious implications it would be comical. The police got on that ship and then got off again because they were not sure where the territorial waters ended and international waters began. We are talking about extending jurisdiction to 200 miles. From all the reports I have heard, this ship was. in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. If I am not mistaken, it was the previous minister of the environment, although I was not in the House at the time, who introduced the headland to headland principle of establishing baselines from which the territorial waters limits were to be set.
On the basis of that headland to headland principle the entire mouth of the St. Lawrence River would be covered. How anyone could have thought that ship, ploughing

through the ice and still within the mouth of the St. Lawrence River-not out beyond Newfoundland, but somewhere between Anticosti Island and Sept-Iles-could have been in international waters I cannot understand. Yet the government, which had Mounties on board to bring that ship back, removed those Mounties for 24 hours, and then put a larger contingency of Mounties back on board when it became sure of its position.
I would draw to the attention of that shipbuilder from Levis that this is illustrative of the lack of direction and understanding by the government of what maritime policy is all about. I am delighted there are members on that side of the House who are in support of this measure. They ought to be sitting on the front benches. How is that for an invitation? I would like to see that, because I think then we would be working in the right direction. Perhaps I may call it six o'clock, and I will be pleased to continue my remarks at the next opportunity.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock we were discussing the comparable programs in respect of Canadian agriculture and agriculture as it might be abroad. We will continue along the same line and take a look at the Australian program. They found themselves not too long ago with a surplus of peaches. These peaches arrived, canned and processed, on the Canadian market. They appeared in stores in Ontario at a price estimated by our peach growers to be less than the cost of harvesting and processing their peaches if sold on the Canadian market.
In contrast to this, at considerable expense people from this continent developed a market for french-fried potatoes in Australia. We still have Australian peaches in Canada, but only in times of acute shortage will there ever be anything but Australian french-fried potatoes on the Australian market, because they made it impossible for our french-fried potatoes to be sold there. They made sure that Australian french-fries were french-fries which were made in Australia. Australia has always protected its farmers in such a way that our situation cannot be considered favourable at all.
One might go on and mention country after country, and product after product which appears on the Canadian market as a result of which the Canadian producer suffers from coast to coast and no deterrent action is taken by our government to relieve the situation. There are no artificial barriers set up to prevent the flooding of our market with foreign produce. We have muddled around a little in respect of the beef industry and the protein industry, as well as with several other industries on this continent, but basically when the whole picture cleared we found that the Canadian producer received the short-end of the horn, yet we were told by the minister that we are better off in Canada than they are in the United States.
If we were to ask if we are better off in Canada than they are in New Zealand or Australia, the answer is obvious. However, as a result of the temperate climatic
Agricultural Stabilization Act
conditions in the United States production costs there are less than they are in Canada. The industrial milk produced in the United States is not produced mainly in the northern areas of the United States but rather in the areas where the climate makes it possible to sustain a herd of milk cattle much more economically than it could be sustained in the northern area of this continent, Canada. It just happens that the U.S. dairy industry can buy hay from Quebec and Ontario at prices which would shock our farmers. They have been doing this for years and producing the milk to supply their market. They are not doing that for their health. Sure, people complain about milk prices from Maine to California, just as there are complaints about this from Prince Edward Island to Victoria.
This is not a country in which farmers have any great pride in respect of government policies so far as their income is concerned. For instance, when the government placed a ceiling on the price of fluid milk it did not distinguish, on a regional basis, what was the cost of milk. A great many milk producers for the home consumption market lost a great deal of money in the province of New Brunswick as a result of an unrealistic ceiling, or too small a ceiling, imposed upon them by pressure from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and not imposed upon them by any force within the province of New Brunswick.
So long as the Department of Agriculture caters to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, both the producers and the consumers will continue to suffer as the result of the extremes of low and high cycles such as we have seen in the last two years.
It is time that the government of Canada became aware of some of the trading necessities and natural trade patterns which could exist in this world if we put agriculture at the top of our list instead of at the bottom. It seems rather significant that today we received a news release from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce that we will spend tens of millions of dollars to subsidize the construction of boats to keep 15,000 people at work. I do not quarrel with the policy which will make it possible to build ships in Canada, but what I do quarrel with is the facade and the sham of an agricultural policy which, in the minister's own words, will reflect upon the income of one third of Canada's people, and the pittance which is being spent and the lip service which is being paid to the industry of that one third.
A serious effort must be made by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to market our agricultural products. In the research branch of the Department of Agriculture we must have an interest in the expansion of our production and a broadening of our products with an eye toward foreign markets which are available.
Since potato producers have been before the minister this week already and representations have been made to him, it is easy to give this as an example. The research branch within the minister's department could introduce to Canada a variety of potatoes which is in very heavy demand in the South American market. This is something for which agriculture in Atlantic Canada has been asking for years, and there is not yet a single seedling of the yellow fleshed potato introduced in Canada which could

Agricultural Stabilization Act
be marketed in vast quantities by a properly developed industry. This is but one example. There are markets for our potatoes which could be exploited on a worldwide basis because the purity of our soil, the climatic conditions under which the seed is grown, and its freedom from disease make our potatoes unique. We have a variety of potatoes which few if any producers can match anywhere in the world. I submit that the quality of our potato industry is tops and the promotion of our industry by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is secondary at best. This is typical of many other things which have happened under this administration.
Canada is being balkanized, in an agricultural sense, as the government tries to pass the ball to the provinces. In your approach to agriculture, an irresponsible approach I might say, why don't you get a pack of cards, boys, and you can enjoy yourselves. This is directed especially to the minister. The balkanization of the agricultural industry is now just beginning, and if it is not arrested by positive government action, the effects on a great many Canadian communities can be serious.
If, for instance, the province of Alberta were to say to every producer in Alberta, "We are going to guarantee you a profit as did British Columbia," and if the province of Ontario were to say-and there was an editorial comment on this, as I am sure the minister will remember-"We are going to guarantee to every farmer every product in our province," what will happen to a great many products grown in a great many other provinces which are not economically capable of competition in that kind of structure?
There was this threat not too many months ago when the Department of Agriculture called on the government of Ontario to show its industrial might, to distribute money in the field of agriculture and to show the rest of Canada that it could play that game too. While that game is being played in British Columbia, there are at least two provinces which have unofficially told their potato growers, "Sell your crop for whatever you can get out of it. We will see that you come out all right". That makes three provinces that are now openly engaged in the promotion of agriculture within their own boundaries, to the detriment of agriculture in the rest of Canada. This is balkanization; it is setting up competition in which communities will disappear. It is encouraging the production of crops which are not natural to some areas, and it will defeat the production of some crops which are natural to other areas and leave them stripped of their economic base.
The threat of the minister of agriculture in the province of Quebec to make Quebec totally self-sufficient in eggs, in potatoes, in corn, in grain and in beef has come directly as a result of the abstinence of the government of Canada from a program of stabilization which was traditional in this country in the first 100 years of its confederation. It has been total neglect, not a sense of responsibility, which has brought this situation about.
Here we have in this bill again, and in the minister's speech the statement that if provinces do not like our payments, the provinces may top load our structure to the advantage of their own farmers. This is inviting disaster. It is inviting another chicken and egg war which was

brought on by the stupidity of the policies of the government on your right, Mr. Speaker. This is inviting another financial debacle in the meat industry, as has happened as the result of encouragement to feed grains to animals for which there was no market. These policies in the past have been directly responsible for the virtual bankruptcy of thousands upon thousands of farmers, and yet we will allow the provinces to top load, if they wish. This does not make much sense with regard to Canadian agriculture.
Now let us consider the bill itself. There are perhaps two or three differences in phraseology, but in effect this bill is the biggest piece of camouflage that has been used by any government in the history of Canada. It even surpasses the camouflage that was exercised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) when he said his policies would cure inflation, because a significant part of this bill is the discretionary clause 7(1). Let me read both clause 7(1) in the bill and the section in the old act.
Section 7(1) in the act reads:
The Board shall from time to time in accordance with this Act take such action as is necessary to stabilize the prices of agricultural commodities at their respective prescribed prices, and shall take such action and make such recommendations as are necessary to ensure that the prescribed prices for an agricultural commodity in effect from time to time shall bear a fair relationship to the cost of production of such commodity.
Bear in mind the formula "shall bear a fair relationship to the cost of production".
Now let us read the bill. Clause 7(1) reads in part:
(b) make such recommendations, including recommendations respecting the index calculated as described in paragraph 8.2(l)(a), as are necessary to ensure that the prescribed prices for agricultural commodities in a year bear a fair relationship to the production costs of such commodities in the year.
Here we have the key phrase of the agricultural policy of price stabilization, and it remains now as it was before at the discretion of the Price Stabilization Board and of the minister in charge because the act requires them to disregard the index structure, if necessary, to obtain a fair price in relation to the cost of production in the year under consideration for any given product. This is not just my opinion. I checked this with lawyers who have better understanding of the law than I do, and each one has said that there is virtually no change in this bill, that it is just a disguise of something old to make it look like something new.
There is one change, as outlined in the minister's speech, and this is one which I resent very much. I think the minister should have consideration for his industry because it has been said that there will be an interdepartmental committee which will help the Department of Agriculture arrive at a fair price which a stabilization program should set.
There is no way that any other department in the government has the capability of arriving at a fair stabilization price to the same degree that the Minister of Agriculture and his staff have. I agree that there is a time and a place for a multi-departmental consideration in respect of policies in agriculture, but I submit that there is no time and no place for a multi-party committee to sit down and decide on a level of stabilization for agricultural products.

The Department of Agriculture presumably knows the cost of production and, according to its records and bulletins, it presumably knows the price farmers are receiving. The Department of Agriculture therefore is qualified as is no one else.
It reflects the fact that the government has not had a Department of Agriculture in a policymaking position since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. This multi-departmental committee would be required to be sure the urban input goes in, not that the rural and agricultural input is the deciding factor, but that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and perhaps the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve), and heaven only knows who else, will tell the Department of Agriculture how much support it should give to a particular product. The minister has shown little cognizance of what is required. Perhaps on that basis he may need help.
It is my understanding that the potato producers of the Atlantic area have already been before the minister and presented their case. It is my understanding that he has said to them that they must prepare themselves with an organization on a regional basis. The implication is that they must have a regulated production and marketing structure. I hope that to substantiate this program the minister will produce evidence to show that Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec will be able to grow exactly the same number of hundredweights of potatoes every year for the next decade so that he can measure anticipated or projected production, and be accurate. Anyone who has ever grown a fruit or vegetable crop knows that this is utterly and totally unpredictable. Fruits, vegetables, and agricultural products in general do not lend themselves to man's management for an exact amount of production. I wonder, when he knows this, why the minister would make a suggestion of this nature to the industry.
I will read a little memo from the Prince Albert Herald, which has just been received:
A member of the executive of the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency (CEMA) said Friday the agency is having serious internal problems and will either succeed or fail during the next month.
As has been mentioned in this House, CEMA is not out of trouble just because a committee met, was cut short, was not allowed to deliberate and could not make an in-depth study. While the egg industry may be controllable, the potato industry would be very difficult to control, particularly in view of the jealousy of individual farmers across Canada as to their own accomplishments and their own productions.
It is none of the government's business whether farmers who are in trouble are organized into the tightest organization in the world or whether they are operating individually. They are still losing money, and they still need help. If they do not plant another crop, the consumer will pay more as a consumer than he ever would have paid as a taxpayer to relieve the economic problems connected with the product in question. The magnitude of the loss to the potato industry is beyond the conception of most hon. members in this House.
Does anyone in this House realize that if the potato farmers of the Atlantic area had never dug a single potato
Agricultural Stabilization Act
in 1971 they would have lost less money than they will lose by digging and marketing this crop in a great many instances? The cost of production has virtually tripled in a period of less than three years. That is the magnitude of the loss those producers will experience, and it is none of the minister's business whether they come one at a time or as a group, because he has said that the government of New Brunswick and the government of Ontario will have to administer matters anyway regardless of how it is done. Let the governments of the provinces deal with each problem as it arises and give the producer a fair shake. Do not tell the farmer what to do. He has enough intelligence to know what he wants to do.
For the first 100 years of confederation we did not have ministers, bureaucrats or anyone else telling the farmer what to do. We did have a Department of Agriculture and a department of statistics which put some information before the farmer which was a help and a guide, but we did not issue orders to him, and we did not tell him he had to have a CEMA or we would not help. That is ridiculous. There are opportunities in this world where surpluses, virtually every food Canada produces, can be put away.
It should be the responsibility of the government of Canada to consider its foreign aid program and to insert our food surpluses into that food program so that Canadian agriculture could prosper and those who are starving could be fed. Instead of that we have an agricultural program which tells producers to cut back, control and manage their markets. What we do not need is a set of rates applied by the government under the Trudeau administration. What we need is a little incentive, a little encouragement, a little help.
Let us consider the potato market in particular. It is in this regard that I have the most serious complaint to lodge against the government and the Department of Agriculture. If one looks at the statistics on production of potatoes in Canada and in the United States, one recognizes the real fact of this situation. There is only one potato market, one beef market, one pork market; there is virtually only one market for every commodity produced in Canada, and that is the North American market.
When one considers the estimates published in the fall of 1974 which show a 14 per cent increase in potato production on this continent in that crop year, the handwriting was on the wall from the day those figures were published. The minister at that time should have known, before the public knew, that the potato industry was in deep, dark trouble, and not just in the Atlantic area. It was in trouble in Quebec, Ontario, and all across the eastern half of Canada. At that time there was a market which, with a little government help, could have relieved Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island farmers of the pressures resulting from loss in the marketing of this crop. But the pressure is being exerted by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It is not coming from the Minister of Agriculture.
In 1971 when P.E.I. and New Brunswick were negotiating for a little assistance for potatoes, we were told we could not take any early action because the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was afraid we might create a shortage and cause a series of high prices again. Only a socialist would ask an idiotic question like that. I regret very much that we have this bill before us in its present form. Certainly I stand for price stabilization. Certainly I stood for the old act. Certainly I stand for the use of the authority under this bill or the other act, and there is no difference.
The only specific difference that I can see is that the word "wheat" has been left out of the named products as though it might relate to wheat grown outside the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board. I should like to know the significance of that. It is not very likely it would come under a stabilization requirement in eastern Canada. Since barley and oats have been specifically named in the bill I wonder why feed wheat in particular, such as is produced in eastern Canada, was not included. I would ask the minister to look into this. Presumably it could be designated, and I think the reference to the authority of the Wheat Board shows that there is an element of doubt.
The agricultural industry has seen prosperity come and go. It has made a lot of money as a result of world weather conditions and not as a result of policies inaugurated under this minister or any of his predecessors in the last ten years. This minister had no control over the appetite of the Japanese while they were enjoying prosperity, nor over the crop failures in Russia which resulted in prosperity for Canadian farmers.
I would agree with the minister that some farmers were never better off than they are today, but there never was a greater policy vacuum in Canada than that which is being created under present leadership. Unless farmers marketed their beef as the minister directed they did not receive the subsidy. Many farmers in New Brunswick with small beef herds never received a nickel of subsidy. When they asked for a subsidy on hogs at a time when they were losing $15 or $20 a hog, they were told that the question would be looked at in April, 1974, which at that time was 14 months away. Mr. Speaker, that is what one would call a vacuum in policy. If it had not been for the provincial governments picking up the tab there would scarcely be a hog farmer left in Canada today.
There is a lack of policy in the agricultural industry, Mr. Speaker; there is confusion and an expansion of the balkanization of Canada. Agriculture should be a federal responsibility, and so should its stabilization. International trade should be designed to protect Canadian agriculture and give it the opportunity to expand. We should not be confused any longer by the platitudes, the jokes and happy smile of the minister while beef producers still lose $70 per animal and the potato market goes down the drain. Mrs. Plumptre complained when a few dozen eggs spoiled-what will she say if millions of hundredweights of potatoes are dumped in this country? That is what will happen as a result of the inactivity of the Trudeau government and its total neglect of agriculture.

speechtext:
The situation that agricultural producers face in Canada today, is not one of their own making. Farmers in this country have been faced with rising costs before. They have been fighting the battle of increasing costs of everything they buy for many, many years. The cost price squeeze on Canadian farmers has been a part of their life for 20 or 30 years and, I am sure, has been the subject of debates in this House. I know it has in many provincial legislatures and elswhere. In the last couple of years farmers have been faced with dramatic cost increases for everything they buy. I need not document them here. Farmers themselves are well aware because they know the increase in price of binder twine, fertilizer, machinery and machinery parts.
Perhaps we as the members of parliament should take more time to document the increase in costs faced by farmers rather than talking to one another in this chamber. I am satisfied that the great majority of Canadians are unaware of the kind of cost increases faced by farmers. The fact that about nine out of ten Canadians, or perhaps more, never get near a farm is one of the reasons for this. If they do have occasion to visit the farm of a relative or a friend they tend to think of farming as it was 10 or 20 years ago. But it has changed, Mr. Speaker.
The industry today is vastly different from the kind of family farm that many of us grew up on; in years gone by farmers could get by with lower returns. If they were producing potatoes in New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island, they could get by if for no other reason than that families and neighbours got together to bring in the harvest. But that day has gone. The mechanical harvester, which costs thousands of dollars and must be paid for over a long period, is the method in general use today.
Bill C-50 contains three improvements over previous legislation. First is the shorter base period, second, the provision to allow co-operation with the provinces, and third, the use of the 90 per cent figure. I have one quarrel with the legislation in a general way though, and that is that it is not specific enough. The bill is primarily enabling legislation and I hope when it gets into committee that the minister will provide greater detail on how the various stabilization plans will function.
I should like to turn now for a few minutes to discuss how this bill will affect the beef cattle industry. I recognize the difficulties faced by the minister and his officials

in implementing an improved stabilization plan for the beef industry because it is more difficult to deal with than the production of potatoes or tomatoes.

Many years ago. I want to congratulate the minister for the job he has done to provide stability in the beef industry. I am the first to admit that the plan is not perfect.
We have heard a great deal of debate, both inside this House and outside in recent months, over the possible loss of revenue and income to oil producers and others associated with the petroleum industry in Canada. To me, the irony of this debate lies in the fact that producers in the oil industry have not lost money. They have yet to lose money. They are worried, because in future they may not earn the high income they want. I do not intend to compare the oil industry in Canada with the beef industry and ask which is more important, because the health of both industries is crucial to the Canadian economy. I merely point out that although we have discussed the oil industry for weeks, that industry has yet to lose money.
The beef industry of Canada, unlike the oil industry, has lost many millions of dollars. Never in the history of Canadian agriculture has there been such a fanatic turn around in prices as has occurred in the last 18 months in the Canadian beef industry. Rather than go into the history of the various developments of the last couple of years, I want to look at the stabilization policy provided for under this bill, and at the $45.42 price level provided for this year.
In normal times, a one-year period from August 12, 1974, to August 12, 1975, might be a reasonable period on which to base a support policy. But I suggest that these are not normal times in the beef industry. They are chaotic times for the producer. They are particularly chaotic for the young farmer or the new farmer in that industry. I suggest that the proposed method of calculating support payments on a 12-month basis will completely fail the beef producer. I therefore urge the minister, as I did the other day in committee and privately, to consider dividing the calendar year, into four months' or three months' periods, or other short periods, in order to bring about equity in possible pay-outs under this plan.
At the end of September the market price for Grade A-l and A-2 beef was around 48 or 49 cents in western Canada. A week or two ago that price had dropped to 35 and 36 cents. Prices, therefore, had dropped by up to 14 cents in six months. If you average prices for the last six months I am sure they would come to about the $45.42 pay-out.
An examination of prices paid at both ends of the six-month period just alluded to will show, I submit, that the man who bought cattle in the fall and marketed them in
Agricultural Stabilization Act
the last six weeks would not receive fair treatment under this policy. These are unusual times and we may have to consider unusual solutions. The grain grower and potato grower can put his products in the bin and store them. The beef producer is not that fortunate.
I will be the first to agree that farmers in western Canada, particularly, have leaned too heavily in the past on finishing cattle with a heavy grain ration. At the same time it simply is not possible for the industry to adjust in a year or two to different approaches to finishing cattle. The sharp increase in barley prices about a year and a half ago took place in the matter of a month. The beef people found it very hard to adjust to such a rapid change.
Let me make one thing clear: I have no quarrel with the increased price received by the grain producer. I do not expect the grain producer to help bear the increased costs of finishing cattle. But grain increased in price so rapidly that the beef producer was put in an awkward position, especially as the price of cattle was declining at home and on export markets and there was a beef surplus all across the world. Incidentally, the beef producer was not the beneficiary a couple of years ago of cheaper grain prices. It was the Canadian consumer who gained most.
I am only repeating what was said to me by beef producers in my constituency as recently as a week ago. We know that feeding and distribution costs have risen dramatically. Increased electricity costs at the plant and larger wage costs at the supermarket have been added on to beef costs. The consumer has paid a larger price. Nevertheless the consumer price has not risen as much as beef costs have risen, and the producer, as a result has been caught in the squeeze. All the people in the beef handling trade have added their costs. This bill is designed to help the producer, but it will not help him unless the minister and his officials are prepared to adjust the time frame within which support programs are to be established. I think we all want to see the producer treated more fairly.
I am well aware of the representations made to the minister by cattlemen's groups and other so-called official organizations representing the cow-calf producer. I point out that over three quarters of the producers in my constituency belong to no official organization. Also, they are not always happy with the representations which have been made to the government about adopting a hands off policy with regard to the beef industry and support programs. They are anxious to see the government introduce programs which will not disrupt the market process. I think we can devise and develop such programs.
It goes without saying that this legislation can be valuable not only for beef producers but for all Canadians. I am happy to support the bill in principle. I hope that policies which emanate from this enabling legislation will help the producer.
There is another criticism I wish to direct at the minister, and it is that these policies must be enacted more rapidly than has been the case in the past. The government must respond more quickly to producers' difficulties, especially as costs are rising very quickly. The minister is determined to help producers. He has said this on platforms in all parts of Canada. I think, therefore, that members of parliament would be performing a greater service if they spoke to groups in Saskatoon, Hamilton,

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-50, which is to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act. I listened with great interest to the comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mclsaac). At the beginning I thought he would develop his argument about farm input costs. I think many Canadians misunderstand this aspect of farming. The minister referred to input costs yesterday, and I hoped he would develop that theme. I think the minister understands just how important input costs are.
If inflation were not rampant, I do not think this bill would have been introduced. I should also like to point out that it is inflation which makes legislation of this kind necessary-that but for inflation it would almost certainly not have been introduced.
The principal features of the bill are embodied in two main clauses, those dealing with the base period and the prescribed rates. In the final analysis one must refer specifically to those clauses. I believe it would be useful at this point to review them and try to understand their intent. If we consider the base period, and proposed new section 8 covers this carefully, we find an amendment stating that the base price of an agricultural commodity in any year shall be the average price at representative markets for the five years immediately preceding. I am sure all members recognize that the existing legislation makes provision for a 10-year period as the basis of calculating the average. I believe it is obvious to all of us that in today's economy, with inflation as we have seen it, a five-year period is not realistic. I cannot understand why the minister did not use four years, three years or some other formula.
Dealing with the question of prescribed prices, the bill states that for "named commodities" the amount of a prescribed price will be determined by-
... adjusting ninety per cent... of the base price thereof for the year by an index... to reflect the estimated production costs of the commodity in the year as compared with the average of production costs for the five years immediately preceding the year ...
I wish to develop this reference to production costs a little later. This is to be compared with the average of production costs for the five years immediately preceding the year. In addition, the index which is to reflect production costs is determined by the cabinet, presumably upon a recommendation of the stabilization board. For "named commodities" the percentage of the base price may be higher than the guaranteed 90 per cent-but, again, only with cabinet approval.

With respect to "designated commodities" new section (8) says the amount of a prescribed price would be determined by cabinet-it is the cabinet which will decide what will be the percentage of the base price. As I understand the legislation this price could be higher than the 90 per cent, but it could also be lower. I think this point should be stressed. Once again the index used with respect to "named commodities" will be the same as that used to determine the cost of production.
In my view the amendments do not provide the protection for the farmer that the minister has implied throughout his speech and, indeed, in speeches made before the bill was introduced. Earlier this week I met with members of the horticultural council and they confirmed my impression that the legislation before us would do nothing more than provide some small measure of help in times of disaster. It would certainly not go any distance toward stabilizing farm income.
I wish at this point to make a few observations with respect to inflation, and in particular with regard to its impact on the farming community. I want to compare the impact of inflation upon our farmers with its impact upon consumers generally. All members will recognize, I am sure, that there has been a great deal of information concerning the effects of inflation on small business, on office employees, on consumers in general. Considerably less attention has been given to the impact of inflation upon the farm community. Yet how could one fail to note the effect of rising costs of fertilizer and farm machinery, to say nothing of the rapidly rising cost of operating such machinery? One of the tragedies of the egg marketing report which was before hon. member recently was that the minister did not see fit to enlarge the committee's terms of reference.
As has been mentioned by other speakers, there has been a lack of communication between the farm community and the metropolitan areas, a failure to draw attention to the magnitude of the increase in farm costs as compared to the increase in the cost of living suffered by consumers in general. In fact if one analyses the inflationary practices at work it is impossible to avoid the conclusion that the clauses in the bill to which I have referred, namely, those dealing with the base period and the price formula, do not reflect today's economic conditions. Let me repeat that in my view the present debate would be redundant and I do not believe the bill would be presented to the House if the government had found satisfactory ways of dealing with inflation.
I wish to refer to farm input price indexes. Farm input price indexes are published quarterly and annually by Statistics Canada on a 1961 time base-the 1961 index equals 100. The aggregate price index is divided into major group indexes, for example, land and farm buildings, farm machinery and motor vehicles, hired farm labour and other farm materials and services. Each of the major group indexes contains more specific component indexes.
The farm input price indexes are designed to measure the movements of prices paid by farmers for inputs into farm production. The indexes are price indexes which reflect only the direct impact of price changes on the cost of purchasing a specified basket of farm operation inputs. It should be emphasized that the indexes are not cost of

production indexes. The latter include not only price changes but also changes in quantities and qualities of input items, and changes in productivity resulting from better management, improved technology, weather conditions and biological forces.
I believe we need clarification from the minister in this area because I find it inconsistent that when dealing with such matters as old age security benefits, the Canada Pension Plan, and contractual agreements between labourers and employers we deal with price indexes, yet in this instance we deal specifically with production indexes which, I suggest, can be substantially lower than the price indexes. I am not confident that this formula truly reflects farm input costs. At some point, either during this debate or in the committee, the minister ought to explain in some detail what appears to be a paradoxical situation, a situation in which the farmer is not recognizing his true input costs.
I realize that statistics often act as a sedative, but I think I should risk quoting certain figures in this instance.
I would refer to the Canadian Statistical Review published by Statistics Canada, for January, 1975. With respect to the base year, the aggregate index-total farm inputs-shows that prices of farm inputs have increased by more than 95 per cent since 1961. Between August, 1973, and August, 1974, the index for total farm inputs increased from 173.3 to 195.2, representing a rise of 12.6 per cent. Over the same period the cost of hired farm labour increased by almost 17 per cent, building replacement costs by 11.4 per cent, and fertilizer by 48.3 per cent. Let us look more closely at the fertilizer situation.
The price index for fertilizer averaged 103.0 in 1972, only 3 per cent higher than in 1961. In 1973, it averaged 115.5, only 15.5 per cent higher than in the base year. The rapid price increase in fertilizer began in late 1973 and by August, 1974, the index was 65.4 per cent higher than its 1972 level.
The price of feed has also increased dramatically above the level of 110 in 1972 to 211 in the third quarter of 1974, an increase in that short period of time of 91 per cent.
I believe this is of some value if we assess the percentage increase in the farm input price index over the period August, 1973, to August, 1974. This is the most recent 12-month period that I could find. The tables show, for example, that the 12.6 per cent increase in total farm inputs was distributed unevenly across Canada-10.9 per cent for eastern Canada and 14.7 per cent for western Canada. Over this 12-month period the majority of large increases in prices occurred in the category of "other materials and services", with the exception of a 38.7 per cent increase in the index for fencing construction and repairs. Rather interestingly-and this supports the argument of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport-the only area in which there was a definite decrease was in the index for feeder cattle, which showed a decline of 27.5 per cent. All other materials and services indices increased significantly.
What are some of these major increases during this 12-month period? Seed was up 81.8 per cent during the 12-month period; small tools and supplies increased 59.3
Agricultural Stabilization Act
per cent; mixed fertilizer, 50.1 per cent; grain seed, 39.2 per cent. Let me give the House an indication of the recent price acceleration. If we take the three month period between the second and third quarters of 1974, in that short space of time the index for petroleum input products increased by 11 per cent, fertilizer by 14.6 per cent, and small tools and supplies for the farming community by 11.6 per cent.
I now want to turn to another avenue to compare costs of farming, and I refer to farm operating expenses and depreciation. When Statistics Canada people make these estimates, they include farm business costs incurred by farmers irrespective of whether they are paid for in cash or are accumulated in new debt. As far as possible these estimates will exclude outlays for goods and services obtained directly from other farmers. Also in the calculations, subsidy payments are taken into account in order that these estimates represent only net amounts paid by farmers.
I should like to review some of the statistics obtained from the "Quarterly Bulletin of Agricultural Statistics", published in December of 1974. If we assess these figures carefully we find that the total operating expenses and depreciation charges of Canadian farmers were estimated at about $4.8 billion in 1973, an increase of 23 per cent above the 1972 value of $3.9 billion. Farmers' outlays for production inputs have been higher in all provinces as a result of cost increases for most expense items. I think it is of interest to note that there is one expense item which was actually down, and this was property taxes. I know that will interest the minister. In 1973 there was a decline in that particular segment which was related to the implementation of the Ontario farm tax reduction program. The only area in which there was an actual drop was in property taxes.
