I know that these statistics may have had a somewhat sedative effect, but I think they are important in indicating the severity of inflation for the farming community. They are extremely important to the consuming public because they give them some of the idea of the impact of inflationary costs on the farming community. It is also important to note in reviewing these figures that farm input costs have been substantially higher than the price increases experienced by the average Canadian consumer as reflected in the consumer price index.
As I indicated at the outset, this present legislation has been introduced simply because of the effects of inflation. As I have indicated, this bill is of no value in view of the inflationary conditions we have today; and in my view this piece of legislation will offer no support, in terms of stabilization, for the Canadian farmer.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as this is the first opportunity I have had of making a speech in this Parliament, I should like, first of all, to congratulate you on the charm with which you perform your duties in this House.

This evening we heard a very depressing speech from the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) which was gloom and doom, hindsight knowledge and very partisan. That is the only comment I will make about it.
If ever there was a group of farm producers who can produce more and, from time to time, whose besetting sin is excess-you are probably aware of it as much as I am, Madam Speaker-it is the producers of potatoes in eastern Canada. In the past, they have benefited from the advantages of the Agricultural Stabilization Act which help all of them have appreciated. The minister is now introducing a bill to improve that act considerably. As the hon. member opposite said, there is an urgent need for it, and I agree wholeheartedly with him.
Hon. members are also aware, Madam Speaker, that eastern Canada potato producers are unfortunately going through a year of abundance, when prices are deflated. The resulting situation, which still persists, brought to the office of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), two

provincial delegations, from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, in the hope of negotiating a solution and perhaps obtaining financial assistance for the producers, at least this year.
I am prepared to give full support to the bill introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. I do not intend to speak at length, but I hope to have soon the opportunity to study thoroughly the bill with my colleague in the Standing Committee on Agriculture. However, if I rise this evening, Madam Speaker, it is because yesterday the minister invited to do so, in answer to a question which I directed to him concerning the discussions which he held with the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island ministers of agriculture.
I am not a farmer nor a farming expert. I have never been either a co-ordinator of the potato industry, as the member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) who was fuming while making his speech this evening. However, I regularly meet in my constituency a great many farmers and others who used to farm but who no longer do so, as a result of the family farm being bankrupted due in many cases to poor production. Those personal contacts have allowed me to realize the extent of the concern for the future of the family farm and potato growing.
I am happy to support the bill on agricultural stabilization which aims at amending the definition of farm commodities and the calculation of basic prices. I believe this could improve agricultural production and constitutes an excellent formula for price support. As the minister said in his speech, this is basically a matter of guarantee, and this is what the producer wants today. In the final analysis, it is a matter of small prices and orderly marketing.
Madam Speaker, the history of the dark years of potato growing in New Brunswick is a real tragedy. I do not believe I am exaggerating in saying this. But it should also be said that there were good years and even some very good ones. I shall not bore hon. members with statistics, even though I have drawers full of them. However, something must be done now, and the Minister of Agriculture is aware of it. After listening to several members who sit with him on this side of the House, the Minister of Agriculture has understood the urgency of the situation and did not hesitate one moment to introduce this excellent bill in the House.
However, does the burden of putting some order in the farming industry of Canada rest only, as the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) has said, on the shoulders of the federal Minister of Agriculture? I do not think so. There may have been and there probably were some mistakes. The federal government may have made some blunders at certain times, but some provincial governments have made mistakes and blunders at least as serious.
The political history of New Brunswick in agriculture is also a near tradegy and I am not exaggerating in deploring the lack of continuity in the agricultural policy of my own province of New Brunswick. Madam Speaker, I only have to say that in five years, New Brunswick has had five ministers of agriculture. Is this the way to plan in the field of agriculture? And the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte, who criticized the federal government so bitterly tonight, was himself co-ordinator in the field of potatoes
March 6, 1975

in New Brunswick for a few months, between occupying a seat in the legislative assembly or in the House, and yet he did not bring any solution tonight. When potatoes are selling as they were last year at $16 a barrel or per 165 pounds at the farm, the provincial government eagerly takes credit for it. But when they sell at the deflated and ridiculous price of $2 a barrel, as they do now, which means at least $2.50 under production costs for most farmers, what do those people do? They come to Ottawa. They beg and cry for help. That is simply not the way to live! As the Minister of Agriculture said in his speech yesterday, it is catastrophic.
The impact of such a tragedy reaches beyond revenue loss, the disintegration of the family farm. A whole way of life is getting lost. New values and probably questionable ones in my opinion, or new socio-economic factors appear and are also very disquieting, certainly so in the eyes of many New Brunswick farmers. Enter the ogre, now called the multinational, which grabs everything on its way, including the family farm. I was told all those things. I also worry about them.
Madam Speaker, my purpose tonight was not to paint a gloomy picture and yet, unfortunately, such are the present conditions of the potato growing industry in New Brunswick. That production always went through ups and downs. People generally go bankrupt and lose everything during "down" periods. If indeed there is a serious problem, we should wonder first and foremost what farmers themselves intend to do. They do talk a lot these days. They frequently meet and have very serious discussions, Madam Speaker. There are rumours of organization. The minister himself talked of organization and marketing boards on several occasions in this House during this Parliament. He did not rule out that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec might have to organize themselves too. With regard to potatoes, all the provinces of eastern Canada should cooperate and work hand in hand. I do agree entirely.

Madam Speaker, I shall be brief, which I am sure will be a surprise to and will please my hon. friends on all sides. I wish to make a few remarks about the legislation. It is historic and also current that some agriculturalists, some of whom are beef producers, are the most vociferous in their opposition to government intervention. They say: leave the market to its own free play; leave us alone because we do not want subsidies and support prices, and the government should stay out of the business. Those are the usual 19th century dinosaur type of remarks. Then when things get bad they are the first people to come down here crying and asking the politicians to intervene. I recall about a year ago that some of the same cowboys from my riding, who were most vociferous against marketing boards and government intervention particularly regarding support prices or subsidies for beef, were the first people who were down here lining up and crying.
All I can say to that kind of agricultural producer, particularly the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley, is that if he is so smart and if the free enterprise open market system is so good, why is it that the free enterprise parties bring in agricultural stabilization legislation? I

Agricultural Stabilization Act

Madam Speaker, I want to say to the hon. member from Saskatchewan that he took me back a few years to when we both did a little cowboying at Walsh. I thank him for reminding me of it.
In my contribution to this very important debate which will determine just what amendments are to be made to the Agricultural Stabilization Act of 1957 and 1958, I want to make a few general comments on the new bill and then follow with some very specific comments on how this act and the proposed amendments apply to the total Canadian cattle industry.
At first glance this bill seems fairly straighforward and might be construed to be merely an updating of the 17 year old act to make allowances for inflation and rapidly rising costs of production in the total agricultural sector in Canada.
I have no great quarrel with the proposals to change the averaging period from 10 to five years, and the increase to 90 per cent from 80 per cent in determining the base price over this averaging period. But because of some very erratic farm prices throughout all of 1973 and the first quarter of 1974, I suggest that there may have to be some shortening of this five year period. In the five year period 1970 through 1974 inclusive there have been about three and a half years of market prices which could be described as moderately increasing farm product prices. This was followed by a year to a year and a half of very sharply increased farm prices in most commodities, including cattle. I suggest that during the same five year period agricultural production costs increased at a much faster rate than did our market prices at the farm gate.
Under clause 3 of the bill, referring to section 8.2(1) of the act, some provision for this serious concern is indeed provided, but it is not clearly spelled out. The bill reads in part, and I quote:
... the Governor in Council may prescribe, of the base price thereof for the year by an index calculated in such a manner as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council to reflect the estimated production costs of the commodity in the year as compared with the average of production costs for the five years immediately preceding the year ...
I ask the question, does an "index of production costs" refer specifically to the CDA's official farm input price

index? If it does then the cattle industry would be short changed because its farm costs, notably feed grains and feed supplements, have risen faster than most other farm costs during this 1970-74 period. What does the term "may reflect" really mean as used in this proposed section from which I quoted? Does it mean may reflect 25 per cent, 50 per cent, or 100 per cent? And does this reference really pinpoint the fact that index of production costs should refer specifically to the commodity in question by name, no matter whether the commodity in question is a named commodity or a designated commodity?
These items must be clearly spelled out. It seems obvious to me that Bill C-50 leaves far too many details and specifics to be determined by regulation. Another example, under the part dealing with other powers, states:
For the purpose of stabilizing the price of an agricultural commodity, the Board may exercise such other powers as are prescribed by the Governor in Council for that purpose.
Does the phrase "such other powers", for example, mean the supply management route for the cattle industry? If this could be inferred, I wish to state most emphatically that a marketing board for the Canadian cattle industry with supply management powers is not the answer to our cattle industry's very serious difficulties, and in fact crisis, today.
Now I wish to relate my comments perhaps more specifically to the cattle industry. We already have two support price policies recently announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) which relate only to our Canadian cattle industry. Last August 11 the fed cattle- that is, fat steers and heifers-support price of $45.42 was instituted, and if deficiency payments are made when the year is up next August, I presume they will be paid under the provisions of the original act. It is important to understand that this price of $45.42 for grades A, B and C was determined by taking 90 per cent of the average weighted price for these three fat cattle grades at the three principal markets in Calgary, Winnipeg and Toronto, and adding to it a cost of production index figure as determined by the Farm Input Price Index. I have been informed that this cost index item amounted to some 154 per cent of the five year average market price for fed cattle.
The beef cow subsidy or support policy of $23.21 effective last November 16 is 100 per cent of the weighted average price of the Dl, D2, D3, and D4 cows over the last five years at the same three principal cattle markets, but without an indexing figure. Possibly there was no indexing figure because this cow support policy will only last until April 30. In both of those government support price policies the critical circumstances of both cow-calf and the feed lot side of the industry were not recognized. This was primarily because the five year period was too long to account properly for the erratic market swings and the escalating farm production costs.
In today's price and cost terms, what I am saying is that a $45.42 per cwt. floor price is small comfort to a feeder whose costs of grain are still 55 cents to 60 cents per pound. On March 1 the estimated actual weighted average fed cattle price, according to my information, was about $46. This means, of course, that unless the fed cattle

market slumps another $2 or $3 over the next five months, no deficiency payment may be made. In my opinion the Canadian fed cattle market has now bottomed out, and in fact has shown some recovery of a dollar or two in the west and perhaps not as much in Ontario, but it does appear that better markets are ahead of us for fat cattle at least. This will further lessen the probability of deficiency payments being made.
With respect to the cow support policy, it seems highly probable that there will indeed be payments made for those eligible. I most certainly agree with the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) who suggested that the fed cattle support policy should be on a quarterly or half yearly basis. I must say I prefer the quarterly basis.
Surely, Madam Speaker, the time has come for governments and cattle producers to face up to, and recognize the real problems in Canada's beef cattle industry and, for that matter, in the American cattle industry as well. In my estimation we simply have too many cows and, as a result, too many feeder cattle. That means, of course, too many calves about to be born this spring. Since 1969 beef cow numbers have increased some 43 per cent, and are still increasing. The new calf crop could be up another 2 per cent over last spring. For the same period the United States has seen its cow numbers increase by 22 per cent.
The reasons for this surplus cow situation are now reasonably well understood. They are not peculiar to Canada or North America, but are global and relate to unusual weather patterns and a switch from the cheap food era to the present era of rapidly increasing food costs. This global switch started about seven years ago and during this seven year interval we made some wrong assumptions. By we I mean farmers, cattlemen, consumers, and most of all, governments. We thought that, because live cattle prices and retail beef prices were rising rapidly over most of the world, there must be a shortage of cattle, especially on this continent.
We completely ignored or forgot to make allowances for three significant factors. First was worldwide inflation; second, devaluation and realignment of some of the major world currencies, and third, the fantastic impact on a global basis of the energy crisis and the resulting balance of payments problems. We really were not short of cattle supplies but we thought we were, and governments must accept a great deal of blame for this error in judgment.
In simple terms we have about a quarter million surplus cows in Canada at present. We need to market about 900,000 cows this year if we are to stop the growth of the national cow herd. Last year we only marketed slightly over 600,000, and that was less than in 1973. In sharp contrast, however, the United States has turned the corner in its cow cycle. Its cow marketing for 1974 was up by some 20 per cent over 1973. That is the reverse of our situation. For that reason the United States will resolve its cow numbers problem quicker than we in Canada.
I want to make a quick comment on the minister's $10 million canned cow beef for foreign aid program which was announced last December 13. I suggest it was a good policy, unique in many respects-perhaps it was even a first-because it proposed to provide a national incentive to reduce our cow numbers and at the same time help the third world needy countries. It was a most welcome
Agricultural Stabilization Act
suggestion but it was much too late-four months too late. It should have been under way last September and have operated all fall at the period of our lowest cow prices throughout the year. It has not helped our cow market at all. This is evident since the deputy minister testified a week ago in the standing committee that to date only sample lots have been canned, and no commercial canning has started although all tenders have been accepted. Perhaps the minister might give serious consideration to a continuation of this policy that would start next September 1.
Earlier, Madam Speaker, I made a comment about supply management and our cattle industry. The alternative to a supply management route for beef cattle must surely be to make our North American market system work as we all know it can work. This means that our border problems involving unequal quotas must be resolved, and soon. At this moment there are over 30,000 more feeder cattle in western Canada than there were last year. We have a total of some 300,000, and that is a record for feeder cattle at this time of the year. Due to extreme soil moisture deficiencies all across the southern prairies the prospects for grass are very poor. In most cases grass reserves, what are left after our mild and open winter, and what new grass we get, will be needed for our cow herds.
Our cattle industry should understand fully the consequences of keeping all these feeder cattle in Canada in the face of empty feed lots-that are not going to be filled for obvious economic reasons-and the lack of summer grazing. Are we going to export feeder cattle or are we going to eat the fat cattle here, later on? If the decision is to eat the fat cattle here, then we had better be prepared to accept prices considerably below the United States level for the next two to three years. The only country in the world that can afford to buy our cattle at North American market levels is the United States.
I say again, Madam Speaker, it is time we resolved our quota problems at the border. Only last week the press reported that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce proposed a meeting with United States trade officials. One of Mr. Butz's assistant secretaries has indicated that they would be pleased to see the quotas ended even if the situation may soon reverse, with Canada's producers anxious to sell their cattle in a higher priced American market.

IMMIGRATION-ALLEGED RCMP INVESTIGATION INTO RACIAL TROUBLE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-POSSIBILITY OF INTENSIFIED PROGRAM OF DEPORTING ILLEGAL ENTRANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday I pointed out to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) that Australia, because of its 6 per cent unemployment, has intensified its program to deport aliens who are in that country illegally. It seems to me that that government is acting on a simple principle-When you have a law, it must be enforced. To do anything else makes a mockery of our entire legal system. Laws of this kind are made to control those who have least respect for the rights of others. Inherent in that fact lies the probability that the people who make those laws necessary are the very people who are most likely to violate them.
I also recognize that our democratic way of life depends on a large reservoir of trust, that most people are in fact law-abiding citizens; but it is the law-abiding people who suffer most at the hands of those individuals who have lost all conscience regarding responsibilities.
Whenever we have laws that lose their meaning because of ineffectual and half-hearted enforcement, we erode the standards by which our citizens guide their conduct. All of us need reference points for our lives. There are times when we face decisions for which we may or may not have a ready answer, regardless of how intent we are on doing right. The law becomes the reference point for our behaviour and gives us the opportunity for moral and psychological rest and equilibrium, as opposed to tension and distress. In short, the law helps us to decide. That is true only if the law is dependable, clear and enforced. But when the government declares a law, then backs off, does not enforce it, does not take it seriously, it places citizens in an impossible situation, a situation of indecision and tension.
If the government declares a law but does not provide for meaningful enforcement or penalties, it declares loudly

that it does not take its own laws seriously. And this is where we find ourselves today.
The amnesty program the government conducted 18 months ago was a clear admission that the government had allowed aliens to flout our laws. The fact that there are still thousands of aliens in our country illegally shows that the government still has not moved in with the muscle that is needed. The immigration officers on duty at our borders are doing yeoman's service, but they are not getting the kind of support they deserve.
The point is that aliens here illegally either take jobs away from the legitimate working force or else are a drain on the social services of our country. Because they are here illegally it is impossible to determine exactly how many of them there are in this country. This fact underscores the need for the government to design more effective machinery for tracing aliens in Canada.
Let me illustrate how they drain the tax dollars allocated to social services. The Toronto Star of February 6, 1975, carries a story about a Guyanese immigrant awaiting deportation, by the name of Chunilall Misir. According to the Toronto Star, the Immigration Department reckons the total cost of keeping Misir here, without medical bills, is around $11,000. In addition he was hospitalized because he had tried to escape custody; he broke his hip and his heel and there are large hospital bills beside the $11,000 bill already incurred.
Then there are those parasites who find ways to get welfare benefits, UIC payments and government grants. Once an individual decides to remain in a country illegally he decides, in effect, to become a law breaker. From that point it becomes increasingly easy for him to violate other legal and ethical boundaries.
This brings me to my third and final point, which is that illegal aliens more easily become a destructive element in our society. As I have pointed out, they already see themselves as violators of the law. This in itself restricts the number of legal avenues open to them. It therefore becomes all too easy for them to drift into a life of furtive relationships and questionable living patterns. I am by no means suggesting that all those who find themselves in this predicament are living in constant violation of other laws, but I am saying that their situation leads all too easily to this kind of lifestyle.
For these three main reasons I should like to cajole the minister until he is ready to beef up the border patrol, speed up the process of hearings and, in short, deal emphatically with this issue so that people may once again believe that Canadian laws mean what they say. I welcome the green paper and the opportunity it provides the Canadian people to contribute to the legislative process, but in the final analysis it matters not how good a policy emerges from these discussions or how good the laws may be if the government lacks the resolve to enforce its legislation.

subtopic: HEALTH-INQUIRY AS TO STANDARDS FOR ASBESTOS FIBRES IN AIR-CONDITIONS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE IN YUKON
HEALTH-INQUIRY AS TO STANDARDS FOR ASBESTOS FIBRES IN AIR-CONDITIONS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE IN YUKON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise pursuant to a question I asked in the House the other day concerning the dangers posed by asbestos, particularly in a Canadian mine over which the Canadian government has sole jurisdiction, namely, the Clinton Creek mine in the Yukon Territory.
To understand this situation one has to look at what is happening at the Thetford Mine in Quebec where it has been found that 61 per cent of 1,200 miners are suffering from lung abnormalities, including two types of cancer and a condition called asbestosis, which ultimately leads to death.
It is interesting to note that in this case the waste asbestos products have been blowing in the air and across the border. The environmental protection agency of the United States found it to be too much for them in Maine, yet the government of Quebec seemed to be quite happy to allow this condition to continue. I recognize that provincial jurisdiction is involved here and I am not charging the federal government with any particular neglect in this area; but I think we now have to concentrate upon those matters that are within federal jurisdiction, since more and more evidence has come to light about the connection between lung cancer, chest cancer, cancer of the larynx and asbestosis.
My information is that in June, 1974, asbestos counts were taken at the Clinton Creek mine in the Yukon. Out of 133 counts, 19 proved to be significantly above the level of five fibres per cubic centimetre. To appreciate the significance of that, Britain's standard is two fibres per cubic centimetre. In the United States it is five fibres per cubic centimetre. Both England and the United States are about to reduce their standards.
Dr. Carneau, one of the acknowledged experts in this whole question of carcinogens, in respect to asbestos has found that .001 is the only safe level. He is from the University of Illinois, and he was recently funded with a $3.5 million grant. No place in this country now has a level
Adjournment Debate
that satisfies Dr. Carneau, yet we have increasing evidence that cancers are developing.
The difficulty is that these cancers do not develop for many years. We have some cases of people being exposed to asbestos for as short a period as four months and developing lung cancer 35 years later. In the Clinton Creek mine, studies since June of 1974 have been in the hands of the minister's department, and what I want to find out is whether he has made any studies of the miners concerned. Have we checked into the number of compensation claims that have been made as a result of this situation and which are under our sole jurisdiction?
The minister's answer, which I submit is a complete red herring, was: "Well, all we have to do is pass the environmental protection act in this House and we can go right ahead and fix it up." He had better look at the environmental protection act, which does contain certain provisions; but we have already passed a law in this parliament which is known as the Clear Air Act, which I recall my friends in the Liberal party were quite successful in promoting in my riding as a very progressive approach to environmental hazards.
I should now like to quote from "Environment and the Law", a publication of Environment Canada:
The Clear Air Act gives the federal government authority to set national air quality objectives and national emission standards where there is a significant danger to health-
In other words, the jurisdiction and authority to act are clearly within that law now. What I am asking the minister and his charming parliamentary secretary to do is to pass immediately regulations under the Clear Air Act setting minimum enforceable asbestos standards right across the country so that we can start protecting thousands and thousands of miners who work under increasingly hazardous conditions. Why I say the hazards are increasing is that the longer we wait, the worse the problem becomes. The more scientific data we accumulate, the more hazards apparently we are exposing our miners to, Madam Speaker.
On the question of jurisdiction, it is clear that we have sole jurisdiction both in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon through the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. We have the clear right to pass regulations now; we do not have to wait for the House to pass the environmental protection act at all. It is not good enough for the minister to come to this House and to say: "Well, you fellows in the opposition are again blocking progress; we can protect these miners if we pass the bill". I say that is a complete cop-out, and I really did expect something better from a minister who has a very good reputation in this House, one 1 respect a great deal as a result of some of the legislation he has promoted.
What I am asking is for some leadership at the federal level. Admittedly there are problems in Quebec and Ontario in terms of enforcement and getting decent standards. But if we provide leadership at the federal level and put forward enforceable asbestos fibre standards right across the country, then we are going to save some lives. This is a pretty important matter. We may save a few lives of people who have been exposed and who will continue to be exposed to this terrible hazard.

March 6, 1975
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-INQUIRY AS TO STANDARDS FOR ASBESTOS FIBRES IN AIR-CONDITIONS AT CLINTON CREEK MINE IN YUKON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a group from the Bureau of Health Hazards and an environmental engineer from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development undertook a survey at Clinton Creek in June, 1974.
The purpose of this survey was to determine the concentration of asbestos fibres in the air at the mine, mill and townsite. Following the on-site survey, several months have been necessary to check on instrument calibrations and to calculate the results. A detailed report is expected to be sent to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development within the next 10 days.
As a result of recent health findings among asbestos workers the department will recommend that workers should not be exposed to average concentrations of asbestos in the air in excess of two fibres per millimetre. This level is identical to that adopted for occupational situations in the United Kingdom and Sweden recently, and is the same as that presently proposed in the United States. This recommendation is in accord with interim target concentration for the prevention of risk to the health of asbestos workers recommended by the International Labour Organization.
Although many of the levels found in the survey at Clinton Creek exceeded this recommended level, modifications in housekeeping and operational methods as well as improvement in the application of local exhaust ventilation systems are expected to reduce the airborne concentrations of asbestos to the desired level.

It should be borne in mind that the levels we have found in the survey are not grossly in excess of the very stringent standard the department is now recommending, and that the average levels we have found in the air at the mines at Clinton Creek are generally below those that we would have considered acceptable even a few months ago.
There are presently no enforceable federal standards with regard to the presence of asbestos fibres in the air of mines and factories. The recommendations from the department to reduce the airborne concentration of asbestos at Clinton Creek can be the basis for further action by the territorial government.
We do not anticipate any problems from airborne asbestos at the townsite at Clinton Creek where the values found in the survey were between zero and 0.04 fibres per millimetre. The Clean Air Act provides a mechanism whereby pollution of the air at the townsite could be controlled if this were necessary. The environmental contaminants bill presently before the House would provide the authority to enable any necessary measures to be taken to protect the health of the public from the release of substances such as asbestos that contaminate the environment.
In reply to the question of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), the figures quoted in the question would seem to refer to the raw data from which time-weighted averages were calculated. The recommend-

ed level which I referred to earlier is a time-weighted average based on eight hours' exposure.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-POSSIBLE REMOVAL OF PICTURE OF QUEEN FROM PRESTAMPED ENVELOPES
POST OFFICE-POSSIBLE REMOVAL OF PICTURE OF QUEEN FROM PRESTAMPED ENVELOPES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am rising tonight with a double feeling of regret-regret at the action of the government, and regret at the less than complete answer afforded me in the House by the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) a couple of weeks ago when I raised this matter.
The monarchy stands at the cornerstone of our life as a dominion and as a free people. Like millions of Canadians I believe that the symbols of the Crown must be kept permanently before our people, both to remind us of our heritage and to warn us against the loss of that liberty and dignity with which the monarchy provides us.
Accordingly I am at a loss to know why the post office has decided that its eight-cent pre stamped envelopes will no longer bear the portrait of Her Majesty, but instead some modern design. The feeble excuse given is that the new design is philatelically superior and much harder to counterfeit. I ask, who in the world would want to counterfeit it?
Bluntly, this is but the latest in a long line of petty insults to the Crown, over which Canadians seemingly have no control, for which the government has no mandate and by which, I believe, the pointy-headed bureaucrats in the public service are steadily eroding the monarchy position in this country. I have no objection at all if the post office wishes to introduce several varieties of stamped envelopes, and for all I care one might even bear the portrait of the Postmaster General.
The point is, however, that the standard definitive of our Gracious Queen should always be available on stamped envelopes for those Canadians who wish to purchase them, for those Canadians who are proud, and indeed who request specifically such envelopes and stamps as their recognition of the Queen as the emblem of our citizenship and the torch of our freedom.
The Postmaster General answered my question in the House on February 19 in a flippant way. He did not seem to want to admit the change was in the works. This is characteristic of the less than straightforward attitude of the government. Since then my friends in the Monarchist League of Canada tell me they have been inundated with inquiries as to why-Why this action-Why this change carried forward by a government which professes devotion to the Crown on one hand and does its best to remove the Crown from public conscience on the other? What does
March 6, 1975

this step accomplish? Why can Canadians no longer buy prestamped envelopes bearing the image of our Queen?
I challenge the minister to back up the government's words with actions. It is not enough to say the stamped envelopes bearing Her Majesty's protrait were available and may just be available again. I beg with him tonight to please millions of Canadians, and to affirm the government's loyalty to our Sovereign, by announcing that the prestamped envelopes bearing the portrait of Her Majesty will continue to be available, along with any other varieties as the department may see fit to print.
If such action is not taken, Mr. Speaker, loyal monarchists across the country will be excused if they feel that the government has betrayed them, and wonder once again about the forces of republicanism in the public service, forces which represent no one except themselves, no policy except destruction of cherished symbols, and no thought except for so-called progress toward anarchy.

I apologize, Madam Speaker. I am rarely on my feet in the House. I listened to the remarks of the hon. member with a great deal of attention. The new prestamped envelope, as he knows, is to be reproduced by lithography in two colours in order to prevent counterfeiting. So far we have been unable by this particular method to come up with a decent reproduction of the Queen of
Adjournment Debate
which we could be proud. We have been experimenting with it, and it is conceivable that once we have perfected it to the degree that it satisfies the quality we think should exemplify the Queen's picture then we would make sure that these are available.
What I object to is that the hon. gentleman seems to feel that loyalty to Her Majesty the Queen is synonomous with the amount of pictures made available across Canada to the satisfaction of the Monarchist League. I have no apology to make to the hon. gentleman pertaining to the great lady whom I have met on several occasions.
I do not think one can measure a person's allegiance to the Queen, or to symbols, or to the House of Commons, or to other traditions which keep this country together simply by preprinted envelopes. I think the moment of truth comes by other means. The fact of the matter is that if I or the government could be accused of playing politics by removing the Queen's picture from the envelope, then the charge would be equally valid against the hon. gentleman who conceivably could be not necessarily expressing his loyalty to the Queen but catering to the members of the monarchist group for political reasons. I think he will have to have enough confidence in the government and the people who are members of the government, including the Postmaster General, and appreciate that we have as much respect and admiration for and loyalty to Her Majesty the Queen of Canada as he has.
